articles.title: Securing Navigation for Trans-Caspian Trade
articles.full_text:
Since 2022, but particularly in 2026, hard maritime security issues on the Caspian Sea have started moving to the forefront.
Until March 2026, the primary threats to developing trade corridors across the Caspian Sea seemed to be inadequate infrastructure and falling water levels. Then Israel targeted Iranian naval assets in the sea, followed in July by a Ukrainian attack on Iranian military shipments in the waterway. Conflict in the Caspian Sea has made it clear that physical maritime security is essential to making the east-west route a viable, reliable alternative conduit for critical resources. 
The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, the east-west route known as the Middle Corridor, provides 4,250 kilometers of rail lines and 500 kilometers of sea connections between Europe and Central Asia, transiting through Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan. The Middle Corridor will also potentially connect further to China via a new rail line through Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan and link Armenia and Azerbaijan through the 42-kilometer Zangezur Corridor thanks to the U.S.-sponsored TRIPP deal. 
A second route, the International North-South Transport Corridor, once developed, would span 7,200 kilometers and connect Russia to the Persian Gulf, via the Caucasus, the Caspian Sea, and India. Conceived more than 20 years ago, the proposed north-south route has gained new life due to Russia’s need for alternative routes since the full-scale war in Ukraine and India’s interest in a route to the Arctic circumventing China.
Both trade routes highlight the Caspian region’s centrality for supply chain resilience and the expansion of connectivity. Nevertheless, many bottlenecks prevent these ambitions from reaching fruition. The World Bank argues that trade along the route could triple by 2030 if ten priority actions are taken immediately. These include improving port infrastructure and rail connections, increasing the quantity of rolling stock, and addressing customs, logistics, and governance challenges.
The declining water level of the Caspian Sea exacerbates these challenges. Russia has been damming the Volga River, which accounts for approximately 80 percent of the Caspian’s water. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Natural Resources attributes the shallowing and retreat of the Caspian Sea to climate change. Although the shallowing began in the 1990s, the water level has declined to a new low in 2026. Higher air and water temperatures contribute to further evaporation. Dredging is a short-term, and expensive, solution and ferry transport – crucial for exports of critical minerals from Central Asia – already has been reduced along some routes. Although the Middle Corridor states are well aware of the problems, with Kazakhstan declaring the dropping water level a state of emergency in 2023, the fossil fuel and maritime industries they depend on further contribute to the Caspian Sea’s shallowing.
The Caspian region also faces geopolitical headwinds. Russia and Iran have historically blocked Caspian pipeline projects that dilute their own leverage on fossil fuel exports. China would seem to benefit from an alternative trade route given the interruptions to other routes that Russia’s war in Ukraine has caused. Some observers see China treading cautiously with the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway to avoid a negative reaction from Russia. 
Others see China’s potential for greater involvement as counterproductive to a trade route for critical minerals that is supposed to provide an alternative to Chinese supply chains. U.S. opposition to a sanctioned Chinese company serving as operator for a new deepwater port of Anaklia on Georgia’s western Black Sea coast, a project seen as important for the further expansion of the Middle Corridor, may have contributed to the Georgian government’s decision to retain control. 
However, since 2022, but particularly in 2026, hard maritime security issues on the Caspian Sea have increasingly moved to the forefront. 
The North-South Vector: Sanctioned Trade and Arctic Gateway
The North-South vector of the Caspian Sea involves conflict-related trade flows between Russia and Iran and a framework for a multilateral trade route involving India. With the Black Sea under Ukrainian attack, Russia’s 2 million tons of annual wheat deliveries to Iran are now being shipped via the Caspian Sea. In 2026, Russia also began sending parts for Geran-2 drones to Iran to replenish its supplies used in the war with the U.S. and Israel. Ukrainian sources allege that Russian-made drones based on Iranian technology have been found in the UAE, indicating Russian transfer of their own production to Iran.
Iran has been shipping ammunition and three types of drones to Russia via the Caspian Sea for the war in Ukraine, as CNA explored in a January 2025 report on the Russia-Iran Relationship. Iran also provided related training and facilitated Russian production of Iranian drones inside Russia. The two countries used “dark port calls” – that is, sailing without using required transponders – to mask their covert Caspian Sea transits. 
Such efforts did little to camouflage the arms trade in the Caspian Sea. Russia has launched attacks on Ukraine from its Caspian flotilla. For its part, Ukraine views Iranian and Russian vessels involved in weapons trade for Russia’s war as fair targets. One Iranian sailor was killed in a July 25 Ukrainian drone attack on a cargo ship. On March 18, Israel attacked the Iranian port of Bandar Azali, its first Iranian target on the Caspian Sea, to disrupt Iran’s supplies of military equipment from Russia.
These attacks raised concerns in India, which signed an agreement with Iran in 2024 to operate the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Chabahar Port on the Gulf of Oman. New Delhi is eager to develop the North-South trade corridor with Russia, Iran, and Caspian states such as Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. India and Russia signed an agreement in December 2025 for partnership in the Arctic, including using the North-South corridor to expand Indian access to the region. Russia has been enthusiastic about greater Indian participation to offset the prevalence of “unfriendly countries” and balance China’s greater activism in the Arctic.
The East-West Corridor: Economic Potential and Security Threats
Since 2022, the Caspian region has grown in importance as a source and transit region for Western energy and mineral resources. 
Energy remains the most important regional export. Over 90 percent of Azerbaijan’s oil and gas production is offshore in the Caspian region. Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, meanwhile, extract most oil and gas onshore and historically have exported it via pipelines through Russia and China. However, even before Ukraine’s systematic campaign against Russian energy infrastructure in 2026, Kazakhstan had increased shipments of oil across the Caspian Sea via the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline to avoid Russian transit, although exports through the BTC pipeline still only account for 2.3 percent of Kazakhstan’s oil production. Turkmenistan, meanwhile, has three gas pipelines toward China in operation, with a long-delayed fourth in the works. Although a long-discussed Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India pipeline remains stalled, U.S. and Turkish officials have spoken highly of a potential subsea Trans-Caspian Gas Pipeline. 
The Trans-Caspian Gas Pipeline, first proposed at least 25 years ago, would connect Turkmenistan to Azerbaijan, and from there continue onward toward Türkiye. Until 2018, the Caspian’s uncertain legal status gave Russia and Iran de facto vetoes over progress. However, the 2018 Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea clarifies the right of the littoral states to lay pipelines and cables through their own sea/lakebed regions, establishing Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan’s right to lay a connector pipe. Iran is finally moving toward ratifying the convention, enabling it to go into force. A realized Trans-Caspian Gas Pipeline, coupled with expanding onward pipelines from Azerbaijan, would offer Turkmenistan’s gas a narrow route to Türkiye and Western markets free of Russian or Iranian control. As noted by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during a recent Senate hearing, this would be “in the best interests of the United States and its allies.”
Central Asia’s global importance is growing beyond just energy. Both the U.S. and the EU have signed agreements, particularly with Kazakhstan, to expand access to critical minerals. For these to reduce the dependence of the U.S. and its allies on adversaries, however, they must make it out of Central Asia. The Caspian Sea is the only route out of the region that does not require transit through Russia, China, Iran, or Afghanistan. The broad Middle Corridor project to build alternative ground links through Central Asia toward Europe has produced some important infrastructure investments, and freight has grown. But more remains to be done, including with the Department of State’s Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund, established in 2026 to catalyze private-sector investment in trade links across the South Caucasus and Central Asia. For example, bottlenecks impeding Caspian Sea transportation require further investments in port infrastructure and shipping. 
Advocates for expanding trans-Caspian transport links in Kazakhstan suggest that it is an important means of risk management, and the cost advantage of traditional Russian routes can be reduced by investment. Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, and Turkmenistan could all benefit from expanding an independent Caspian Sea export route, but they would be wise to focus on securing the route. The value proposition for these states, global investors, and the U.S. and its allies is to diversify trade routes away from Russia, in particular. However, Russia and Iran have both repeatedly demonstrated their capacity and willingness to disrupt maritime traffic and infrastructure important to Western or global supply chains. Threats could range from anchor drags and sabotage to mine-laying, interdiction, or military attacks. Such threats would require only modest capabilities to address. 
Central Asia offers an important alternative source for critical minerals and energy for the global economy. In recent years, the U.S. and Europe have clearly recognized this. However, realizing Central Asia’s potential to diversify Western sources of critical raw materials requires secure navigation across the Caspian Sea. Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan, and Kazakhstan should each – and ideally, collectively – focus on maritime monitoring and presence as cross-Caspian trade expands. Ashgabat, Astana, and Baku have already invested in new platforms, including uncrewed systems. Targeted US and European security cooperation with these states should focus on building and sustaining capability that makes the most of new systems. This offers a clear and targeted way to enhance Caspian security and address its old and new security challenges, thus facilitating the sustainable development of the Caspian trade corridors. 
The views expressed are those of the authors and do not represent those of CNA or its sponsors.

articles.title: Vietnam Sentences 11 to Death in Country’s Largest Ever Drug Trafficking Case
articles.full_text:
The case dates back to March 2023, when four flight attendants were ‌caught carrying narcotics hidden in toothpaste tubes on a flight from Paris to Ho Chi Minh City.
A Vietnamese court yesterday sentenced 11 people to death and 19 to life imprisonment in one of the country’s largest ever drug trafficking cases.
The case dates back to March 2023, when four flight attendants for Vietnam Airlines were ‌caught carrying narcotics hidden in toothpaste tubes at Ho Chi Minh City’s Tan Son Nhat International Airport, after arriving on Flight VN10 from Paris. The tubes contained more than 2.9 kilograms of ketamine and 8.3 kilograms of MDMA.
The Ho Chi Minh City People’s Court yesterday sentenced 11 people to death for illegal drug trafficking in connection with the case. This included the alleged ringleader Ha Danh Nam, 52, from Nghe An province, who remains on the run and is one of four defendants being tried in absentia. All 11 were also fined between 50 and 100 million dong ($1,916 and $3,832) each.
Prosecutors allege that Nam “organized the transportation of drugs from France to Vietnam by air and through international express delivery services,” disguised as consumer goods from France into Vietnam, according to the state media outlet VnExpress. They said that drugs “were concealed in toothpaste, dietary supplements, confectionery, and other consumer goods.”
Members of the network then used delivery services, encrypted messaging platforms such as Signal and Telegram, and bank accounts registered under other people’s names in order to distribute the drugs throughout Vietnam while evading detection.
Among the 19 defendants who received life terms was Hoang Sy Thang, 39, and his nephew-in-law Bui Van Anh, both also from Nghe An, who ran the network’s main storage point and were convicted of the illegal transport of narcotics.
According to a report in VnExpress, the so-called VN10 case was “the largest drug case in the country’s history, with transaction flows traced at nearly VND29 trillion ($1.1 billion) across close to 500 branches and sub-branches in 34 provinces and cities.”
A total of 227 defendants were subsequently charged in connection with the case. In addition to the trafficking and transporting of drugs, the charges also included possession, use of forged documents, concealing a crime, failure to report a crime, and unlawful appropriation of property. However, the four flight attendants avoided criminal charges after investigators ruled that they were not aware of what the toothpaste tubes contained.
The 11 death sentences in the VN10 case could be among the last that Vietnam hands down for drug trafficking. In recent years, the government has narrowed down the use of capital punishment as part of a broad overhaul of its Penal Code.
Last month, the government recommended removing the death penalty for an additional six offenses, among them drug trafficking. The death penalty for illegally transporting narcotics was similarly removed last year, along with seven other offenses.
If approved at the National Assembly’s next session in October, the latest revision to the Penal Code would leave the death penalty in place for just four crimes:  treason, murder, terrorism, and the illegal production of narcotics.
While the death penalty remains in place for the charge of drug trafficking for the time being, it remains to be seen whether these sentences will be carried out before then – and if not, whether the change will apply retroactively.

articles.title: Japan’s FOIP 3.0: Is Pragmatism That Delivers Resilience Enough?
articles.full_text:
Japan’s updated vision is sharper and more self-interested.
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae meets with Vietnam’s President and Communist Party chief To Lam, in Hanoi, Vietnam, May. 2, 2026.
When Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae visited Vietnam in early May this year, she presented an “evolved version” of the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP), a key plank in Japanese foreign policy, which is being called FOIP 3.0. The “Updated FOIP” specifies as priority areas “Building economic infrastructure for the age of AI and data,” “Co-creation of economic growth opportunities through public-private collaboration and rule sharing,” and “Enhancing cooperation in the field of security to ensure regional peace and stability,” each with its own items for concrete cooperation.
The FOIP was first proposed by the late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo in a speech in Nairobi in 2016. The keyword for FOIP 1.0 was “connectivity,” reflecting the fact that it was launched in the middle of a major shift in the power balance triggered by the rise of China.
International division has only deepened since, following the outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian war, and with the rise of the Global South, international politics have become more complex still. It was in response to this that then Prime Minister Kishida Fumio proposed the New Plan for a FOIP, or FOIP 2.0, in 2023, along with the keyword “inclusiveness.”
Building on this foundation, the keyword for FOIP 3.0 as proposed by the Takaichi administration is “resilience.” With any improvement of relations with China unlikely in the near time, and with the United States pursuing an exceedingly unpredictable foreign policy under Trump, Japan faces what might be called a double risk. It needs to deepen cooperation with Indo-Pacific countries to mitigate those risks and ensure autonomy and resilience. The new FOIP is thus heavily shaped by the imperative to revitalize the Japanese economy and strengthen economic security through cooperation with the Global South, including the ASEAN countries.
The idea of connecting Japanese growth strategy, economic security, and Global South strategy has been clear enough since the Kishida administration. That administration adopted the New Policy toward Enhanced Cooperation with Global South Countries in June 2024. It also implemented institutional schemes to strengthen cooperation with the Global South, such as launching the Global South Future-Oriented Co-Creation Project and Official Security Assistance (OSA) as well as reforming the Official Development Assistance (ODA). The Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) is another scheme launched under that administration. However, whereas FOIP 2.0 emphasized Japan’s ideal international order and its commitment to that order, FOIP 3.0 does not define an order as explicitly; instead it pushes a pragmatism that more clearly emphasizes economic renewal and the restoration of Japan’s vitality.
The three priority areas specified in the FOIP 3.0 each list their own spheres for concrete cooperation. They are the 17 strategic fields identified by the Council for Japan’s Growth Strategy established under the Takaichi administration, areas in particular where Japan wants to promote development, with special emphasis being placed on AI and semiconductors, digital server security, and information and communications, quantum technology, and other fields that are relevant to digital hegemony.
What the times may call for is precisely this kind of pragmatism: an emphasis on revitalizing the Japanese economy and strengthening economic security in the name of “resilience.” Resilience has become an equally important theme for the ASEAN countries as they navigate what one might call the “geoeconomic turn.” Confronted with Trump tariffs, the energy supply disruptions from the Strait of Hormuz crisis, and related pressures, they have become increasingly interested in cooperation to mitigate geoeconomic risks. Key to surviving this uncertainty will be each ASEAN country’s ability to connect its national interests and resilience to broader cooperation across the region. Through FOIP, Japan aims not only to cooperate with individual ASEAN countries but to support ASEAN’s collective efforts to build resilience, contributing to risk mitigation across the region.
Japan can no longer rely on overwhelming economic power and technological advantage as the basis for cooperation with ASEAN countries and other parts of the Global South. There are limits to cooperation built solely on the pragmatism of shared gains. For Japan to earn the trust of ASEAN countries and others in the Global South, it must also clearly demonstrate its commitment to a rules-based international order capable of constraining the arbitrary actions of major powers. Japan is advancing concrete initiatives, but it must also clearly articulate the worldview behind FOIP — the kind of order it is trying to build — in light of today’s upheavals.

articles.title: Escaping the Escalation Trap in the Thailand-Cambodia Maritime Dispute
articles.full_text:
Compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS could help both sides insulate sensitive negotiations from domestic political pressure.
A detail of a British admiralty chart of the Gulf of Thailand published in 1957, which shows the island of Koh Kut.
The Gulf of Thailand forms the second axis of the Cambodia-Thai border dispute. The 27,000-square-kilometer Overlapping Claims Area has been disputed since 1972 and is estimated to hold some 1.6 billion barrels of oil and 17 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Thailand terminated the 2001 memorandum of understanding governing talks over the OCA in early 2026, after fighting along the two nations’ disputed land border in July and December 2025. The outbreak of war reignited historic territorial and political animosities between the two Southeast Asian states and resulted in a border closure that still persists.
The immediate cause of the fighting was a calculated political leak by Cambodian Senate President Hun Sen of a private 17-minute telephone conversation with Thai Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra. The recording exposed Paetongtarn adopting a deferential posture toward Phnom Penh while offering critical remarks regarding her own military commanders.
As Hun Sen no doubt intended, the political fallout in Bangkok was swift. The leak locked Thai political elites into a severe audience cost escalation trap, where public outrage severely restricted their diplomatic flexibility. Paetongtarn’s political credibility evaporated almost overnight, and a wave of hyper-nationalism culminated in her suspension and removal from office by the Constitutional Court. Domestic political discourse in Thailand became thoroughly militarized, effectively ending any immediate possibility of bilateral compromise with Cambodia.
Riding this surge of populist anger, Anutin Charnvirakul and his Bhumjaithai Party secured victory in the February 2026 election. Anutin formed a hardline government that explicitly prioritized security, deferring border management directly to military commanders. Fulfilling a key electoral pledge to his nationalist base, Anutin’s cabinet formally approved the unilateral termination of the 2001 MoU. For nearly 25 years, the agreement had provided the only framework for maritime boundary delimitation and joint energy development between the two neighbors.
To justify scrapping the agreement without a formal exit clause, Thai legal strategists invoked Article 56 of the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, claiming an implicit right of denunciation based on Cambodia’s alleged failure to engage in negotiations. But the move was motivated above all by domestic politics: it was intended to project strength and to signal to voters that the legacy of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, under whose administration the 2001 MoU was originally drafted, was officially over. However, by dismantling the agreement, Bangkok simultaneously destroyed the remaining institutional safeguards governing the maritime boundary.
Phnom Penh responded immediately to Thailand’s unilateral exit. Condemning the move as a breach of international legal obligations, the Cambodian government announced it would initiate compulsory conciliation under Annex V of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). It was a shrewd political move. Having suffered a military defeat on the land border and remaining in an inferior position to its Thai counterpart, Cambodia was also facing increasing pressure from powerful states due to its domiciling the online scamming industry. Hun Manet engaged in forum shopping, choosing a legal avenue that promised low cost and high potential reward. By choosing compulsory conciliation, Cambodia has demonstrated its resolve to be a “good member” of the international community, pull Thailand into a non-binding, low-sovereignty-cost legal mechanism, and demonstrate to the Cambodian people a willingness to “stand up” to a superior opponent.
While compulsory conciliation might initially appear to exacerbate tensions, international legal design suggests that it could provide a necessary off-ramp for both countries. Under Annex V, proceedings are transferred to an independent five-member Conciliation Commission. As international relations theory emphasizes, third-party delegation fundamentally alters political dynamics by depoliticizing interstate friction. By placing complex maritime claims in the hands of neutral legal and hydrographic experts, the framework insulates negotiators from the volatile domestic audience costs that previously constrained leadership in both Bangkok and Phnom Penh.
Crucially, Annex V compulsory conciliation produces recommendations that are non-binding. This flexible design lowers sovereignty costs for both state parties, reassuring their leaders that participation does not entail an irreversible loss of national jurisdiction or offshore resources. In other words, the framework functions as an essential political circuit breaker. It introduces mandatory procedural time delays that allow hot-headed nationalist fervor to cool, while offering political elites a neutral, international body upon which to shift blame for necessary diplomatic compromises.
The practical viability of this mechanism was demonstrated in the landmark Timor-Leste v. Australia conciliation in 2016. In that case, Annex V conciliation successfully bypassed entrenched jurisdictional exclusions and deep bilateral hostility over the Greater Sunrise gas field. Furthermore, conducting confidential proceedings in the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague coupled with a 12-to-18-month cooling-off period provides essential procedural insulation. This shields negotiators from volatile digital news cycles and interrupts short-term electoral mobilization, allowing executive leaders to escape the audience cost trap.

articles.title: Indonesia’s President Pitches His Country as Russia’s ‘Gateway’ to Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Prabowo Subianto described his country as “a natural entry point to ASEAN” for investors.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and Russian President Vladimir Putin take part in a plenary session at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Russia, Sept. 3, 2026.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto yesterday described his country as Russia’s gateway to Southeast Asia, as he pushed for closer trade and investment ties between the two nations.
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin, Prabowo urged Russian businesses to invest in Indonesia, stating that the Pacific should become a “highway between our two economies.”
“For Eurasian businesses, Indonesia is a natural entry point to ASEAN,” Prabowo said, according to a report by the Straits Times. He described the two nations as having ” very profound and important historical ties that have lasted for more than five decades” and said that Moscow was “an important partner” for Jakarta.
Prabowo apologized to Putin for having skipped the ASEAN-Russia Commemorative Summit in Kazan in June, which was attended by leaders from 10 of ASEAN’s 11 member states, and joked that he was paying off my ‘debt’ now by coming to Vladivostok.” Prabowo also extended an invitation for Putin to visit Indonesia at some point in the future.
In his own address at the EEF, which was established in 2015 with the aim of drawing investment into the underdeveloped Russian Far East, Putin emphasized the importance of Russia’s relationship with Asia in general and Indonesia in particular. He said that the Asia-Pacific “is a powerful centre of growth and sets the pace for the development of the entire global economy.”
“Russia is an active participant in investment and trade cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region,” he added. “We interact as equals with our partners and with the region’s leading integration groupings.”
Putin also told Prabowo that he regarded Indonesia as “one of Russia’s trusted friends in ASEAN.” Prabowo was the EFF’s main guest of honor, a year after he was accorded the same privilege at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum.
Prabowo’s trip to Vladivostok is the second trip he has made to Russia this year, following a visit in April, and the fifth time that he has met with Putin since taking office in late 2024.
All of this testifies to the recent growth in the relationship between Jakarta and Moscow, albeit from a relatively low base. Bilateral trade came to just $4.8 billion in 2025, up 21.7 percent from a year earlier, according to Indonesian statistics cited by the Straits Times.
However, both sides seem to believe that there is a lot of unfulfilled potential in the relationship, and have taken substantial steps to augment their trade, investment, and security ties. Since Prabowo took office, Indonesia has joined BRICS and signed a free trade agreement with the Russia-dominated Eurasian Economic Union, a grouping that also includes Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan. The two nations also upgraded their relationship to a strategic partnership in December 2025.
Russia’s bid for closer defense, economic, and nuclear relations with Indonesia is a clear attempt to strengthen its influence in the Global South and reduce the effectiveness of Western efforts to isolate the country since its invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. For Indonesia, a closer relationship with Russia is an important component of Prabowo’s policy of assertive non-alignment, which seeks improved relations with nations of all geopolitical persuasions.
In a post on X, Indonesian Foreign Minister Sugiono said that Indonesia’s participation in the EEF “reflects our commitment to deepening mutually beneficial and concrete cooperation including in trade, investment, energy, and other strategic sectors.”
He added, “Guided by our independent and active foreign policy, Indonesia will continue to engage with all partners and build bridges across regions to deliver tangible benefits for our people, Indonesian Foreign Minister Sugiono said in a post on X.

articles.title: The Japan-Thailand Relationship: Light and Shadow
articles.full_text:
The benefits and vulnerabilities of deepening interdependence
The relationship between Japan and Thailand is closer than ever. Interdependence across economics, security, and human exchange has deepened, bringing shared benefits and opportunities alongside new challenges in the form of supply chain vulnerabilities and transnational crime. Understanding the Japan-Thailand relationship today requires a clear view of both its “light” and its “shadow.”
Diplomatic relations between Japan and Thailand date to the 1887 declaration of friendship (officially, the Declaration of Amity and Commerce Between Japan and Siam), with the 140th anniversary falling in 2027. The two countries have built a close relationship grounded in a long history of exchanges and warm ties between their imperial and royal families. Economic ties deepened dramatically after World War II, and in recent years cooperation has extended to shaping international trade rules, as evidenced by Japan’s support for Thailand’s OECD accession.
At the Japan-Thailand Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in June 2026, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and his Thai counterpart Sihasak Phuangketkeow confirmed that the two countries would enhance their Comprehensive and Strategic Partnership and deepen cooperation under the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) initiative.
Light: Creating Rules in an Unstable Economic Order
Thailand is one of Japan’s biggest manufacturing hubs in Southeast Asia and a key investment destination. Foreign investment in Thailand (on an approved-investment basis) rose by about 68 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, with Japan among the top investors alongside Singapore and China. As U.S. protectionism disrupts the international economic order, maintaining free and fair trade rules has become a shared challenge for Japan and Thailand.
Emblematic of this is Japanese support for Thailand to join the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development). Thailand is pursuing structural reforms that include deregulation, anti-corruption measures, and digital trade rule development. Japan has confirmed it will continue to support Thailand’s accession review. Thailand’s convergence toward the transparent institutions and fair competitive environment the OECD calls for is not merely a matter of bilateral gains; it is an endeavor to build fair and liberal economic rules together. Thailand’s accession would directly improve the business environment for Japanese companies there through relaxed foreign investment regulations and smoother digital trade.
Shadow (1): The Geopolitical Risks of Interdependence
Deep connections, however, have a downside. The most immediate is the direct impact of geopolitical risk. During the Thailand-Cambodia border conflict, which broke out in May 2025, the Thai military blocked border checkpoints, severing cross-border supply chains. In the border town of Poipet, Japanese manufacturers including NHK Spring, which sews car seat covers, and Toyota Tsusho were forced to halt operations at their local sites. Companies were forced to reroute via maritime transportation through Vietnam, reportedly tripling costs in some cases.
Even since the ceasefire at the end of 2025, blockades and tensions have persisted. The hardest hit have been companies that had adopted a “Thailand-Plus-One” strategy, keeping Thailand as their core base while distributing processes into neighboring countries. The deeper the interdependence, the sharper the vulnerability when disruption strikes. It was this reality that also drove the two foreign ministers’ June agreement to promote cooperation in making energy and resource supply chains more resilient.
Shadow (2): Criminal Activities as a Downside of Mobility
More serious still are the criminal activities born of the downside of human mobility. The online scam compounds set up along the Thailand-Cambodia border have produced a steady stream of cases in which people from multiple countries, including Japan, have been confined and forced to take part in criminal schemes. Financial losses from organized fraud in Japan surged to around 325.7 billion yen in 2025, 1.6 times the previous year, some of it linked to operations run out of Southeast Asia.
Japan itself has also emerged as a destination. In November 2025, managers of a massage parlor in Tokyo were found to have employed a 12-year-old Thai girl; the managers were arrested on suspicion of violating the Child Welfare Act and the Labor Standards Act. The girl had been forced to perform work involving sexual content. The trial of the former operator is ongoing as of the end of August 2026. The case exposed the fact that Japan, too, can be a destination for human trafficking. Japanese and Thai nationals alike can find themselves as either perpetrators or victims, and transnational crime is no longer an issue that either country can address alone.
The two countries have begun to respond to these challenges through law-enforcement cooperation. The Japanese National Police Agency dispatched a local information liaison officer to Thailand in June 2026, strengthening joint efforts to crack down on scam organizations in Southeast Asia. At the June foreign ministers’ meeting, the two sides also confirmed they would work closely together on regional issues including the Cambodia border situation. As the flows of people, goods, and money deepen, ever-closer collaboration will be needed to manage their side effects. The true value of the Japan-Thailand relationship ahead of its 140th anniversary lies in whether both countries can build on a long-standing friendship while confronting both its light and shadow together.

articles.title: The Climate Crisis Is Stretching the Nepali Military Beyond Its Limits
articles.full_text:
The question here is not whether the military should be involved in disaster response, but how the military itself is responding, adapting, and transforming amid the climate crisis.
The footage of the avalanche that triggered devastating floods along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers near the China-Nepal border on August 26 is deeply sobering. The road, bridges, customs, and immigration office with China, and the entire settlement and traditional bazaar along the riverbank, were wiped out in a moment. 
In the wake of the flood, the Nepali government deployed security forces, including the Nepal Army, Nepal Police, and Armed Police Force, as first responders. Nepal has put more than 20,000 security personal into responding to the disaster, possibly the largest such deployment since the aftermath of the 2015 earthquake. The collapse of local and provincial governments and the inaccessibility of flood-affected areas prompted the government to rely on the security forces at a desperate moment. 
The use of security forces in disaster response is not new in Nepal. Security forces often get involved, ranging from rescue and relief operations to rehabilitation activities. The Nepali Constitution 2015 (2072 BS) enshrined a provision for deploying the military in national crises arising from disasters and development projects. The National Security Policy (2016) also considers climate change and the environment as part of the national interest. 
But the ad hoc stretching of the security forces into disaster response can result in the security forces themselves being increasingly exposed to vulnerabilities and capacity constraints amid the climate crisis in Nepal. As environmental disasters become more frequent and severe in the Himalayan region, the recent flood must be an important case study in the growing complexity of the military’s engagement in disaster governance and preparedness. 
The scale and intensity of the recent flood was unimaginable and it is becoming evident that there were significant casualties among security forces. A week since the incident, and a total of 85 security force members – encompassing 45 from the Nepal Army, 28 from the Nepal Police, and 13 from the Armed Police Force – are still unaccounted for. 
The police forces went missing while on duty near the border, customs area, and river corridor. Some Nepal police personnel went missing due to a sudden surge in flooding while circulating a notice to downstream communities. Similarly, Nepal army personnel were on duty at Langtang National Park and were stationed at multiple hydropower projects. Armed police forces went missing from a border post. In addition, three police posts in Timure, Rasuwagadhi, and Syafrubesi were damaged or swept away. 
The unique circumstances of the flood gave security personnel very little time to respond. The absence of an early warning system and the lack of any cross-border disaster communication made the situation even more complicated.  
Rescue operations are still ongoing, particularly in areas with multiple hydropower tunnels, such as Upper Trishuli-1, Rasuwagadhi Hydropower, Chilime Hydropower, Langtang Khola, and Upper Trishuli-3A. Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped in these tunnels. As the days pass, families of those trapped and even security personnel are increasingly frustrated. Some tunnel rescue operations have been halted due to a lack of progress and the rescue team’s inability to advance. The security forces are exploring their options, including conducting a controlled blast to clear debris blocking the tunnel. 
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah, speaking at parliament on September 2, said that “tunnels present a very distinct problem, they are filled with mud, debris, and floodwater. Clearing them requires specialized skills that none of the countries, including Nepal, have had. Though we have mobilized at short notice, and progress depends on weather and drier conditions.” He added that the security forces should be commended for their efforts, made under various constraints. 
Footage of Nepal Army personnel laboring and displaying their willingness to risk their own lives in a tunnel operation has drawn attention. The security forces have been widely praised for their courage and bravery. But an emerging consensus has made it clear that the Nepali government, including the Nepal Army, lacks the advanced expertise, technology, and equipment for effective tunnel rescue operations.  Bravery is not a substitute for preparedness, equipment, and expertise. 
The Nepali government has sought international assistance in specific areas, including tunnel rescues and forensic work, and reached out to countries like India, China, and South Korea for critical equipment and technology. This, however, highlights Nepal’s disaster vulnerabilities and preparedness deficits. 
The recent flood reiterates the changing environmental security landscape in the Himalayan region. The International Center for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has identified dozens of potentially dangerous glacier lakes in the Hindu Kush Himalayan region; the recent floods may be less of an outlier and more of a warning. 
The climate crisis, and the use of security forces in response to climate-driven disasters, decisively alters the strategy, function and operating environment of military institutions. The question here is not whether the military should be involved in disaster response, but how the military itself is responding, adapting, and transforming amid the climate crisis. This is particularly important in Nepal, where the military institution is deeply embedded in disaster response and preparedness already.   
The footage of the avalanche that triggered devastating floods along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers near the China-Nepal border on August 26 is deeply sobering. The road, bridges, customs, and immigration office with China, and the entire settlement and traditional bazaar along the riverbank, were wiped out in a moment.

The National Security Policy (2016) also considers climate change and the environment as part of the national interest.

As environmental disasters become more frequent and severe in the Himalayan region, the recent flood must be an important case study in the growing complexity of the military’s engagement in disaster governance and preparedness.

The security forces are exploring their options, including conducting a controlled blast to clear debris blocking the tunnel.

The security forces have been widely praised for their courage and bravery. But an emerging consensus has made it clear that the Nepali government, including the Nepal Army, lacks the advanced expertise, technology, and equipment for effective tunnel rescue operations.  Bravery is not a substitute for preparedness, equipment, and expertise.

articles.title: Australia’s Broken Hill: Where Children Are Sacrificed to Mining Interests
articles.full_text:
A historical mining town in Australia’s outback is confronting severe lead-contamination health threats, disproportionately affecting Aboriginal children.
Mining in Broken Hill persists despite ongoing lead poisoning of children.
Broken Hill is an Australian mining town steeped in history. The town’s legacy of union struggles for workers’ rights is chronicled through street plaques, protected heritage buildings, and murals reminiscent of early-20th-century Mexican muralism.
Under the expansive grey sky over Broken Hill, enormous mining wealth has been created – stretching from Australia to northern Chile and further. As with most forms of wealth, it is rooted in human hardship. In Broken Hill, mining wealth has been accumulated at the cost of children’s exposure to lead contamination. 
Last July, Australia’s New South Wales (NSW) state government, which includes Broken Hill, announced AU$37.3 million (approximately US$26.74 million) to address lead contamination. The funding, as stated in the announcement, will lead to a “twofold increase in the number of homes remediated annually, including the removal of lead-based paint to eliminate lead contamination, the installation of grass to trap dust, and enhanced monitoring of emissions from existing mines and other localized dust sources.”
In Broken Hill, emissions from mining and smelting are the primary source of exposure. Elevated blood lead levels among local children signal a public health crisis. The announcement “underscored a commitment to protect children and families from the long-term effects of lead exposure.”
The funding announcement follows a January 2026 report on reducing the health and environmental impacts of lead contamination in Broken Hill. The NSW Office of the Chief Scientist & Engineer (OCSE) issued the report. “A long history of lead mining in Broken Hill has left a legacy of widespread contamination and human exposure,” said Professor Hugh Durrant-Whyte, OCSE’s NSW Chief Scientist, in the report.
“While some progress has been made in reducing environmental lead levels and community exposure, improvements have slowed in recent years,” he added. “Delays in effective intervention risk irreversible impairment and potential lifelong complications across successive generations.”
NSW Minister for Health Ryan Park described the AU$37.3 million as an “investment” to “help reduce the risk of harm, particularly for young children and infants.” He added, “To see blood lead levels declining among young children screened in Broken Hill is very pleasing. Still, we know more needs to be done.”
Broken Hill is 1,100 kilometers west of Sydney, approximately a two-hour flight. According to 2020 data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), it has a population of fewer than 20,000, of whom 6 percent are aged 0-4 years. Broken Hill is the birthplace of the mining giant BHP and is built on the world’s largest deposit of lead, silver, and zinc. 
Lead mining began in 1885. The first inquiry by the NSW government into Broken Hill’s poisoning dates to the early 1890s. “Lead is a metal that has been mined in Broken Hill for many years,” stated Lead Smart Broken Hill, an NSW public health initiative and community education campaign.
“Lead dust is found in Broken Hill’s dust, soil, dirt, and rainwater tanks, among other places,” according to the Broken Hill Lead Surveillance Program 2023 Annual Report. “It is harmful to people of all ages, but the risk is highest for unborn babies, infants, and young children.”
Cate Faehrmann, an Australian environmentalist and politician, has long been a critic of the NSW government’s lead remediation measures. “Every year we get another report showing Broken Hill children are being poisoned by lead, and every year the government expresses concern,” she said. “It is a national shame that Aboriginal children in Broken Hill are still twice as likely to have dangerous levels of lead in their blood.”
The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that “[l]ead exposure was attributed to more than 3.5 million deaths globally in 2023, primarily due to cardiovascular effects.” It also emphasized that “lead exposure can pose significant health risks for children. When children are exposed to very high levels of lead, it can cause serious damage to their brains and central nervous system, leading to symptoms such as coma, convulsions, and, in extreme cases, death.”
The primary concern is childhood neurodevelopment. Lead affects the central nervous system, kidneys, blood chemistry, and reproductive organs. It impacts children’s cognitive development, and the resulting cognitive impairment can persist into adulthood. The WHO said that lead exposure can also cause irreversible damage to children’s brain development, leading to increased antisocial tendencies and lower educational achievement. 
The 2023 Broken Hill Lead Surveillance Program Annual Report found that approximately 35 percent of non-Aboriginal children and a staggering 68 percent of Aboriginal children tested had blood lead levels exceeding the national public health guideline of 5 micrograms per deciliter.
“One in three Broken Hill kids under 5 have blood lead levels higher than the national guidelines,” said Faehrmann. 
Aboriginal children and families may face barriers to accessing remediation programs, healthcare, and nutritional interventions, further increasing exposure risks. “No child should have to suffer lifelong health impacts because governments won’t stand up to powerful mining interests,” she said.
At the announcement last July of the AU$37.3 million to address lead contamination, Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said: “A long history of lead mining in Broken Hill has left a legacy of contamination that we need to manage better.”
However, the contamination is not merely a matter of better management. It is about neglect or “inaction,” as Richard Weston, chief executive of the Maari Ma Health Aboriginal Corporation, put it. Maari Ma and the Broken Hill Environmental Lead Program monitor lead levels in Broken Hill’s air and soil. They also conduct blood lead tests on children under 5.
“There’s virtually zero interest from the NSW government in the health and well-being of Aboriginal children in Broken Hill,” Weston said. “It’s a waste of time, really.” He added that the funding did not address the inequalities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous children.
Maari Ma withdrew from the Broken Hill Environmental Lead Response Group in November 2025 in protest against “the government’s inaction” and questioned why the NSW government has not adopted a targeted strategy to address Aboriginal contamination and structural injustices.
Weston sad that “structural inequities persist and contribute to lead exposure among Aboriginal children, and that targeted action is required because Aboriginal families have limited access to social housing and rely more on lower-quality private rental housing.” He added, “There’s a strong link between blood lead levels and the quality of housing in Broken Hill.”
Broken Hill faces an acute shortage of affordable housing. This unaffordability forces Aboriginal families to live in uninhabitable, lead-contaminated rental properties. These properties are contaminated by mining activities, exposing children to blood lead levels twice those of the general population. 
Weston noted that although lead remediation in homes is ongoing, the housing situation for Aboriginal people remains precarious, citing substandard housing, overcrowding, and unstable tenancies.
He has called for more social housing for Aboriginal people. He said that unless Aboriginal children have secure housing, they will continue to have elevated levels of lead in their bodies. “Aboriginal children in Broken Hill deserve clean homes, safe air, and a future free from the legacy of lead.”
Broken Hill is an Australian mining town steeped in history. The town’s legacy of union struggles for workers’ rights is chronicled through street plaques, protected heritage buildings, and murals reminiscent of early-20th-century Mexican muralism.

articles.title: Ezra Jin Is Free, But There Are More Pastors in China Behind Bars
articles.full_text:
“I respectfully ask the international community to stand with me – to fight for the freedom of Pastor Gao Quanfu, Pang Yu, and all peaceful Christians imprisoned in China. ”
Pastor Gao Quanfu and wife Pang Yu in an undated family photo.
This July, a miracle took place in China, when Ezra Jin, an imprisoned Christian pastor from an unregistered house church, was suddenly set free. Throughout his 266 days of imprisonment, the international community rallied behind Pastor Jin, culminating in his release.
I write this article in desperate need of one more miracle. My father, Pastor Gao Quanfu of the Light of Zion Church, and my mother, Pang Yu, remain behind bars. My father faces 12 to 13 years in prison on baseless charges of fraud. As their trials approach, I can only hope that the international community will similarly support their cause.  
For my parents, faith and service were a calling. My father became a Christian at age 28, at a time when public religious practice was nearly nonexistent in China. He served as a minister for 40 years: mentoring the next generation of religious leaders, carrying out ministry work, and supporting families in his congregation. He was also a talented musician; he played an instrument called the suona horn. My mother had a successful career as an actress, TV anchor, and producer. It was love at first sight for the two of them, and they anticipated a bright future for their family and community. 
In 2025, my parents paid a steep price for their faith. On May 16, authorities in Xi’an arrested Pastor Gao and eleven other members of the Light of Zion Church. Initially, my father was charged with “using superstition to undermine the implementation of the law.” The charges were later altered; he is now facing charges of “fraud” for accepting voluntary donations from his congregants. Three weeks after my father’s arrest, my mother was detained, simply because she is married to Pastor Gao. 
My parents’ ordeal is reflective of a wider crackdown on unregistered house churches in China. The Light of Zion Church, and other such entities, have drawn Beijing’s ire due to their refusal to submit to state surveillance and restrictions that can include controlling the content of sermons. Although some practitioners have since been released, my parents, Pastor Tang Bingyi of the Light of Zion Church, and eight members of Pastor Jin’s congregation (Zion Church) remain in prison.  
My father continues to maintain that Christian churches should respect the governing authorities, but he believes that his church must preserve its autonomy and biblical convictions regarding worship, doctrine, and church governance. Even as his church endured deepening surveillance and pressure, the congregation responded peacefully – with prayer rather than hostility, and faith rather than fear. 
What my parents are going through is unimaginable. They languish in overcrowded conditions, with more than a dozen detainees in one cell. They are not allowed to communicate with or visit family members. Authorities closely monitor their visits with legal counsel, adversely impacting their ability to freely communicate with their lawyers. 
My parents are almost 70 years old; both have severe health concerns, yet their meals are nutritionally insufficient, and their medical needs are left untreated. I am terrified of what might happen next.   
After more than a year in detention, my parents’ cases are underway – and the potential outcome is chilling. At my father’s pretrial hearing on August 10, we learned that he could be sentenced to 12 or 13 years. We await my mother’s pretrial hearing, and potential sentence, with trepidation. Without a groundswell of international support, I fear that my parents will spend the rest of their lives in prison. 
I respectfully, but urgently, ask governments and policymakers around the world to stand in solidarity with my parents. To the consulates and embassies in the PRC: please show up at their trials in Xi’an, China. Visible engagement and interest from foreign diplomats will signal that the represented countries protect freedom of belief and religion. It will send a message to Beijing that the world has not forgotten Pastor Gao Quanfu, Pang Yu, and other Christians detained in China. 
I cannot be there, so I plead with all those who can to attend. Bear witness and remind my parents that they are not alone. 
My mother and father devoted their lives to me and their congregation. Now, they are elderly, sick, and need me, but I cannot do this alone. I respectfully ask the international community to stand with me – to fight for the freedom of Pastor Gao Quanfu, Pang Yu, and all peaceful Christians imprisoned in China. 
I am proud to be my parents’ son. One day soon, I hope to be reunited with them, to hear my parents play music and sing together again. Even if it takes a miracle – be it political or preordained – I will not rest until my parents walk free.

articles.title: The Meaning Behind Pakistan’s First Lunar Rover
articles.full_text:
The Jinnah 1 mission signals increased cooperation with China and takes Pakistan’s rivalry with India to new heights – literally.
An early prototype of the track system for Pakistan’s first lunar rover, dubbed the Jinnah 1.
The lunar South Pole has emerged as a major focus of international space exploration due to its scientific potential. In view of this, Pakistan has also decided to send its own scientific mission there. The country’s first indigenous lunar rover, Jinnah 1, will head to the Moon’s South Pole in 2029 aboard China’s Chang’e 8 mission. 
Pakistan’s decision to undertake a lunar mission reflects three key perspectives. First, the gesture is symbolic as Islamabad also wants to be among the group of elite member countries conducting scientific research on the Moon, indicating its growing interest in the space sector. Second, the mission signals the revival of an old rivalry on the Moon, as India reached the lunar South Pole with Chandrayaan 3 in 2023. Lastly, Jinnah 1 illustrates increasing cooperation between Pakistan and China in the space domain. 
Jinnah 1 aims to explore and study the geological characteristics of the lunar surface and conduct key experiments for future lunar research. The rover is likely to weigh around 35 kg and have an expected price tag of approximately 400 million rupees ($1.4 million). It will have a panoramic camera, ground-penetrating radar, and a device to analyze minerals in lunar soil using infrared spectroscopy. It will also be equipped with a device for taking soil samples, analyzing and separating the noble gases contained therein, and storing them.
Before analyzing why Pakistan decided to send its own lunar mission, it is equally important to understand why different states are sending their own expeditions to the Moon’s South Pole. The region is believed to be suitable for long-term human habitation due to its vast, untapped ice reserves. If the surface contains large quantities of ice, it can be used not only to produce hydrogen fuel for deep-space propulsion but also to provide drinking water for humans residing there. This will exponentially reduce costs for future lunar and interplanetary explorations. Moreover, it is also an area with elevated ridges, making it an ideal site for generating solar power and for constructing permanent structures that support human presence on the Moon.  
Jinnah 1 reveals Pakistan’s renewed interest in the space sector and the country’s desire to become part of the leading states carrying out activities on the Moon for peaceful purposes. The country is taking this seriously as Pakistan seeks to broaden its space cooperation, using science, research and technology partnerships to build a knowledge-based economy and develop a new generation of engineers, scientists and innovators. 
For instance, Pakistan’s senior government minister, while meeting with aerospace companies during a visit to Houston in July 2026, aimed to deepen the country’s collaboration with the U.S. space agency, NASA. He said that Pakistan aims to launch its first national mission to the Moon by 2035 as part of a broader drive to advance the country’s space program. 
The landing of Chandrayaan 3 near the lunar South Pole in August 2023 made India the fourth country to achieve a soft landing on the Moon and the first to land near the South Pole. The achievement generated domestic and international recognition. Jinnah 1’s targeting of the same lunar South Pole is not coincidental. The rivalry between India and Pakistan – which has been fought on land, in the air, over water, and in the domain of nuclear deterrence – has now acquired a new frontier. The rover’s name, invoking the founder of Pakistan, is deliberately juxtaposed with an Indian achievement named after Vikram Sarabhai (India’s Vikram lander).
The announcement of Jinnah 1 also confirms that cooperation between China and Pakistan extends beyond the military domain, as evidenced by deepening bilateral ties in space exploration. This is not the first space collaboration between the two “iron brothers.” China has launched various Pakistani satellites into space, including the country’s inaugural lunar satellite, ICUBE-Q and the indigenous electro-optical satellites E0-1, E0-2, E0-3, and PRSS-1 – all in the last two years. 
Besides, earlier this year, two Pakistani astronauts completed advanced assessments in China for a human spaceflight mission. One of them is expected to travel to Tiangong, China’s space station, later this year. Pakistan was also the first country to deploy and benefit from the Chinese navigation system Beidou. 
China-Pakistan space cooperation, in short, is a manifestation of the peaceful use of space technologies. Space cooperation between Beijing and Islamabad is likely to increase in an unprecedented manner given the trajectory of their current joint endeavors. 
For Pakistan, the sector offers more than pure scientific exploration. Space-based assets can provide assistance and solutions to Islamabad’s environmental challenges as the country faces severe impacts from climate change despite contributing less than 1 percent of global emissions. 
Jinnah 1’s journey to the lunar South Pole in 2029 reiterates Pakistan’s official stance of exploring celestial bodies for peaceful purposes and refraining from any action that could lead to the militarization of space. The mission signals that Islamabad’s ambitions in space are anchored in scientific contribution rather than in staking a geopolitical claim over the untapped resources present on the Moon.

The mission signals that Islamabad’s ambitions in space are anchored in scientific contribution rather than in staking a geopolitical claim over the untapped resources present on the Moon. 
The lunar South Pole has emerged as a major focus of international space exploration due to its scientific potential. In view of this, Pakistan has also decided to send its own scientific mission there. The country’s first indigenous lunar rover, Jinnah 1, will head to the Moon’s South Pole in 2029 aboard China’s Chang’e 8 mission. 
Pakistan’s decision to undertake a lunar mission reflects three key perspectives. First, the gesture is symbolic as Islamabad also wants to be among the group of elite member countries conducting scientific research on the Moon, indicating its growing interest in the space sector. Second, the mission signals the revival of an old rivalry on the Moon, as India reached the lunar South Pole with Chandrayaan 3 in 2023. Lastly, Jinnah 1 illustrates increasing cooperation between Pakistan and China in the space domain. 
Usman Haider has an MPhil degree in Strategic Studies from the National Defense University, Islamabad, Pakistan. His articles have been published in The Diplomat, Australian Institute of Affairs, South Asian Voices, South China Morning Post, Real Clear Defense, and many others.
Abdul Moiz Khan works as a research officer at Center for International Strategic Studies, Islamabad.
articles.summary: The Jinnah 1 mission signals increased cooperation with China and takes Pakistan’s rivalry with India to new heights – literally.

articles.title: US Allies in Asia Are Paying for the Iran Stalemate
articles.full_text:
The U.S. administration lacks the willingness to confront China and Russia over their assistance to Iran, and Asian allies are paying the price.
M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) conduct live-fire missions during Operation Epic Fury in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility, Feb. 28, 2026.
While the United States still has military options available against Iran, these are unlikely to isolate Tehran from its allies. Despite a new round of sanctions, the regime remains defiant. The key issue for the current administration is that it lacks the willingness to confront China and Russia over their assistance to the regime, and is instead urging Beijing’s cooperation as it looks ahead to Donald Trump and Xi Jinping’s meeting on September 24.
Under the current stalemate, Washington’s allies in Asia are disproportionately affected, at a time where they are being asked to take on a greater share of the regional deterrence burden.
Both China and Russia continue to materially aid Iran and are alleged to have provided intelligence assistance that helped it strike American bases across the region. China has provided drone components, navigation modules, chemical precursors for missile propellant, shoulder-fired systems, and continues its purchases of discounted Iranian crude. Russia has supplied upgraded drones built off Iran’s own design from its Alabuga factory in Tatarstan, along with satellite imagery and damage assessments enabling strikes on American assets. 
The entities involved have been sanctioned, yet they have adapted. Washington has designated Chinese companies, sanctioned tankers and warned banks against dealing with the refineries in Shandong province that import and process Iranian crude. Beijing responded by shifting to overland routes through Pakistan and Central Asia, and by issuing a blocking order that exposes any company obeying the American sanctions to Chinese penalties for doing so.
Both Washington and Beijing have pulled their punches, proving they value their trading relationship more than they do the outcome of the Iran war. After the October 2025 summit, an American export control rule covering the subsidiaries of blacklisted firms was suspended, and China lifted its export controls on critical minerals. In March, oil sanctions on both Moscow and Tehran were eased in response to soaring energy prices. The reciprocal tariff suspension runs until November 10. 
Beijing, for its part, has legally defended its refineries only far enough to pass the risk to third parties. It has not retaliated directly, and it has kept state-owned companies away from the trade so that it need not protect them. This provides a cheap arrangement, which it can abandon at will.
Washington has much to lose and little to gain from further commitment in the Iran war, and Iran’s leverage rests on having correctly assessed how much each side is willing to spend on a resolution. The United States therefore cannot compel Iran by intensifying strikes or enforcing tougher sanctions. It has to reorient Iran’s backers away from it.
The current administration’s unwillingness to do this has overwhelmingly affected its allies in the Indo-Pacific. 
Asia’s reliance on oil imports transiting the Strait of Hormuz has placed countries like Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines in a situation where their interests are a secondary concern for the United States in the Iran war – and remember, the entire conflict already ranks behind its trading relationship with China on the administration’s priority list. If Washington expects industrialized democracies to carry a growing share of the Pacific deterrence burden, then it must recognize the difficult position they now have.
The lack of willingness to impose costs on authoritarian adversaries for aligning their interests has been visible in the northern Pacific, with China and Russia conducting joint drills that North Korea has sought to join. Unopposed, this kind of alignment creates the condition for normalized cooperation between authoritarian states. Allies in the Pacific will remain reliant on the United States, but they now understand that American commitments must be priced in terms of commercial convenience.
For countries in Southeast Asia, the war is predominantly an economic issue that has increased shipping costs and disrupted price stability for energy importers seeking to sustain export-reliant economies. While these states also value security against Beijing’s coercive policies, the incentive to engage with Washington is weak as long as carrier task groups are being rotated out of the region, and the stability of energy markets is in doubt. Pressuring them to align or increase their share of the deterrence burden while not providing much in return is unlikely to yield positive results.
In March, the Atlantic Council recommended that Trump confront Xi directly for his country’s support of Iran. This was a solid suggestion, yet without diplomatic pressure being applied consistently, there is no signal that Washington needs this war over or that it will not tolerate outside support for Tehran. Confrontation has had an effect in the past; it forced Beijing to move to less efficient overland supply routes specifically to avoid naval interception and secondary sanctions. If the U.S. takes no further action, Beijing will conclude that it has correctly calibrated its support for Iran: not enough to provoke a reaction and not so little that Tehran feels isolated.
Furthermore, as long as there appears to be an incentive not to impose costs on China or Russia, allies in Asia will have to prepare for a long-haul period of high energy prices with no clear solution in sight, while their adversaries face few consequences for aligning their interests. Washington’s current campaign against Asian economies it accuses of transshipping Chinese goods to bypass tariffs highlights how much more it seems to value its commercial relationship with Beijing. Punishing allies for routing Chinese goods while leaving China untouched looks a lot like shooting the couriers. Breaking away from this pattern requires a concerted effort aimed at pressuring Tehran’s backers, and that begins by signaling that the November 10 renewal for tariff suspension on China is not guaranteed.
