articles.title: As the World Nomad Games Come Home, Japarov Expands Kyrgyzstan’s National Story
articles.full_text:
The opening of the games coincided with Kyrgyzstan’s 35th independence anniversary and a major Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.
A group of tourists pose in Bishkek’s central Ala-Too square on Aug. 31, hours before the World Nomad Games got underway.
Kyrgyzstan marked 35 years of independence in grandiose fashion on August 31. More than 20 world leaders arrived in Bishkek throughout the day ahead of a landmark Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit, before the curtain rose on the sixth World Nomad Games with a glamorous opening ceremony in the evening. 
Considering the games’ moniker as the “Olympics of the nomadic world,” the spectacle more than befit the occasion. It took place at the city’s newly built 51,000-seater Bishkek Arena, the largest stadium in Central Asia, and featured an impressive array of dignitaries, such as Russia’s President Vladimir Putin and India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The event was reminiscent of the 2012 Summer Olympics in London in its blend of national culture, history, and showmanship. 
Including a lengthy pre-show program, the ceremony lasted nearly seven hours. It began with a series of performances by some of the biggest names in Kyrgyz music, young and old. Then came the 18 heads of state, each personally welcomed by President Sadyr Japarov, with every greeting shown on screens around the stadium. 
Then came the Kyrgyz national anthem, a processional roll call of the 104 countries taking part in this year’s games, and a speech by Japarov, who theatrically rose out of the floor via an elevator platform before delivering his remarks. At that point, there were still nearly 2 more hours’ worth of ceremony to go. 
What followed was a vast dramatic journey through Kyrgyz and nomadic heritage, consisting of a succession of dance routines put on by some 3,000 performers and 300 horsemen, and a non-stop background show of glitzy visual effects. 
The show depicted a variety of scenes, from the symbolic collection of water at Issyk-kul to an episode that ominously appeared at first to represent the Mongol invasion of Kyrgyzstan. (However, the would-be conquerors were eventually revealed to be athletes looking for a game of Kok Boru, one of the country’s traditional sports.) 
Altogether, the performance was impressive in its ambition and exhilarating in its execution — and that was before it was capped off with a fireworks show and short concert given by Nicole Scherzinger from the Pussycat Dolls. 
In many ways, the ceremony encapsulated a broader tendency of the games: conceived by Kyrgyzstan’s government in the early 2010s as a way to improve the country’s image abroad, they have also helped refashion its national identity at home.
“Following coups in 2005 and 2010, and that year’s violence in Osh, Kyrgyzstan was most commonly associated with inter-ethnic tensions, conflict, and other negative things,” Dr. Arzuu Sheranova, an independent researcher based in Germany, told The Diplomat.
“Although the government was initially skeptical of the idea, [they realized] eventually that the games could be used to attract foreign investments [and] rebrand the country as a safe destination for foreign tourists,” she explained. 
What followed was a model, if not entirely intentional, case study in nation-building. Because the Kyrgyz government began to emphasize nomadic self-branding so heavily when preparing to welcome an international audience during the Nomad Games in 2014, 2016, and 2018, the campaign ended up having significant knock-on effects domestically.
“20 years ago, nomadic culture was viewed as backwards, generally looked down upon, and, for the government, was not at all a priority,” Sheranova said. “But the emphasis on nomadic and ethnic elements helped fuel a boom in Kyrgyzstan’s fashion industry, and nomadism and ethno-themed culture have since become a movement in both men’s and women’s fashion.”
Eventually, she said, this nomadic identity surpassed the government’s long-standing official vision for the country, Kyrgyz Jarany, or “Kyrgyz citizen,” which promotes a shared civic identity and emphasizes multi-ethnic social co-existence, and makes little mention of nomadic heritage. 
According to Dr. Shairbek Juraev, a political scientist who heads Crossroads Central Asia, an independent research institute based in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Jarany was also born of the Osh interethnic violence in 2010, and is similar to how “Kazakh” is used in neighboring Kazakhstan to refer to ethnic Kazakhs, while “Kazakhstani” denotes citizens of the country more broadly. 
But while Kyrgyz Jarany is supposed to make room for Kyrgyzstan’s national minorities, “such as Uyghurs or Uzbeks,” Juraev said, “it is pretty much dead,” thanks in part to the “turn towards increasing the role of Kyrgyz language” that has taken place under the Japarov presidency. 
Indeed, signs of the cultural phenomena described by Juraev and Sheranova appeared at Monday’s opening ceremony. Many of the locals, who made up the majority of the estimated 29,000 people in attendance, were dressed in ethno-themed clothing in Kyrgyzstan’s national colors, or in both.
In a similar vein, Japarov began his speech by praising Kyrgyzstan’s “past, present and future.” He hailed the convergence of events on August 31 as an appropriate way of both marking 35 years of the country’s independence and “glorifying” the legacy of the “nomadic civilization” created by its citizens’ ancestors. 
Beyond these references to history, however, Japarov’s remarks were more focused on the present. The 10-minute speech featured a catalog of major forthcoming government-supported projects, such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway and the Ala-Too ski resort.
That emphasis on development was fitting, given how the games have served as a deadline for major infrastructure initiatives. The Bishkek Arena, for example, is now Central Asia’s largest stadium, having been completed just days before it hosted the opening ceremony. Similarly, the hippodrome in the lakeside resort town of Cholpon-Ata, which hosts most of this week’s sporting events, has been renovated to accommodate 10,000 spectators. 
Manas International Airport, the country’s largest, has also undergone major reconstruction, while roads around Issyk-kul have been upgraded, including a new 15.64-kilometer, four-lane ringroad around Cholpon-Ata designed to ease congestion.
In this sense, the games have offered Japarov an opportunity to showcase a country being physically transformed under his watch.Juraev and Sheranova say that is no small coincidence, given his plans to participate in Kyrgyzstan’s upcoming presidential elections in January 2027. 
“[Japarov] and his team will make every effort to take advantage of all these big events as an illustration of how well the country is doing when it comes to the campaign later on,” Juraev told The Diplomat. 
“In Kyrgyz culture, people organize feasts when everything is okay, when they are economically stable; it is an indication that everything is good, and only when everything is good can you have a feast,” Sheranova agreed.
“And the games are a feast at the national level — what Japarov’s administration is doing right now is demonstrating the results of his work during his first term,” she said.

At that point, there were still nearly 2 more hours’ worth of ceremony to go.

articles.title: To Secure the Natuna Sea, Indonesia Needs More Than New Ships
articles.full_text:
Maritime security is one of Indonesia’s most demanding defense domains. And at its current stage, Indonesia needs significant help.
Illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing is one of Southeast Asia’s most persistent maritime security challenges. Indonesia, the owner of the region’s largest maritime area, has expanded patrols in its most contested waters, added community surveillance, and expanded international partnerships to address the threat. As the world’s largest archipelagic country, maritime security is one of Indonesia’s most demanding defense domains. And at its current stage, Indonesia needs significant help. 
The North Natuna Sea, which lies along the southern portion of the South China Sea, is a hotspot for commercial fishing. Home to over 750,000 tons of fish stock, is among the areas where China’s sweeping South China Sea claims overlap Indonesia’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ). Yet despite stepped up maritime law enforcement by Indonesia’s Ministry of Maritime Affairs and Fisheries (KKP), illegal activities – including, but not limited to, IUU fishing – continue.
Indonesia is not starting from zero. Since the 2019-2020 confrontations near the Natuna Islands, the government has expanded the Indonesian Navy and Maritime Security Agency (Bakamla) patrol programs, incorporated fishermen and community surveillance into maritime surveillance through the Kelompok Masyarakat Pengawas (POKMASWAS) program, and distributed communications equipment to selected fishermen communities. Yet these initiatives remain unevenly distributed and insufficiently connected to the agencies responsible for verification and enforcement.
Indonesia still faces substantial capacity limitations. In 2025, only three of the seven KKP patrol vessels assigned to the broader WPPNRI 711 area could reach the North Natuna Sea. Even when the KKP is able to catch IUU fishing boats in the act, there aren’t enough dock space or facilities to store impounded vessels and accommodate the crew. Jakarta began addressing those shortages this July by announcing ten new Class I surveillance vessels and an expansion of the PSDKP pier in Batam, which will become the principal base for operations in WPPNRI 711. 
Indonesia’s partners have likewise invested in its maritime capacity. Japan, for example, through a 9.053 billion yen grant (USD $56.57 million) is funding an offshore patrol vessel for Bakamla, scheduled for delivery in 2028. Other Japanese programs have trained Bakamla personnel in boat operations, maritime law enforcement, criminal investigations, and instructor development. Australia’s current strategic partnership plan with Indonesia provides for fisheries surveillance cooperation, maritime domain awareness information sharing, technical training, coordinated patrols, and desktop exercises. 
In early August, at the Southeast Asia Cooperation and Training exercise in Singapore, Indonesian personnel joined representatives from 15 other Indo-Pacific countries in practicing the real-time transfer of sensor data and vessel-contact information among operational centers, patrol aircraft, and ships. Days later, Bakamla hosted Malaysian and Singaporean coast guard personnel for a trilateral exercise in the Riau Islands covering cooperation in the Natuna Sea. Bakamla Chief Vice Admiral Irvansyah subsequently proposed expanding that model to other ASEAN countries. 
However, a shared regional maritime security architecture is only reliable as the national systems that feed information into it. Exchanging satellite tracks, radar data, or participating in joint exercises are meaningless if fishermen’s observations are unable to reach Indonesia’s national surveillance and enforcement system in time. 
In June, local Indonesian fishermen spotted foreign vessels conducting IUU fishing in the North Natuna Sea within Indonesia’s EEZ. The fishermen reported the sighting to patrol officers, and Indonesia’s Navy deployed the KRI John Lie-358 warship on extended patrol the following day. By the time the warship searched the area the following morning, however, the vessels had disappeared.
Government Regulation No. 13 of 2022 already provides for an integrated national maritime security and safety information system, alongside joint and coordinated patrols. Bakamla Regulation No. 2 of 2024 goes further, directing the system to improve connectivity among maritime information sources, accelerate the transmission of information about security incidents, and support more effective patrols. The legal foundation exists, but Indonesia still needs to develop a standardized operational procedure to ensure that reports reach the appropriate enforcement asset without losing critical hours along the way.
Bakamla’s command-and-control center should maintain a joint reporting and coordination process with designated liaison officers from KKP, the Indonesian Navy, the Water Police, and relevant local authorities. This center would be responsible for interagency communication and assignment, acting as a dedicated maritime desk manned through a single radio frequency and hotline for fishermen to report to. 
Jakarta should also create a Natuna-wide inventory to accurately identify key needs and distribution gaps and ensure that resources are given to those who need it most, both from a domestic perspective and as a reference point for allies when investing in resources. Capitalizing on the Prabowo administration’s recent investments in the Natuna Red and White Fishing Villages, these new hubs could act disbursement centers for communication materials while conducting training for basic vessel identification guidance and report standardization.
Indonesia’s partners should organize their assistance around this chain. Japanese-organized training could help develop watch officers and instructors capable of processing contact reports and integrating the new Bakamla vessel into joint operations. Australian information sharing and desktop exercises could test the full sequence from a fisherman’s initial report to verification and deployment. Future exercises should measure reporting, verification, and response times – not simply whether participating agencies can exchange data.
Once the system functions domestically, Indonesia can make it the foundation for regional cooperation. The next exercise with Malaysia and Singapore should begin with a simulated report from a fishing vessel, require Indonesian agencies to verify and task a response, and then test the transfer of the contact if the suspected vessel crosses into another country’s jurisdiction. Indonesia could subsequently use its position as secretariat of the 11-country Regional Plan of Action to Combat IUU Fishing to promote a common contact-report format and standardize procedures for transferring verified vessel information across borders. 
More patrol vessels will give Indonesia greater reach. They will not matter, however, if those vessels continue arriving after the target has disappeared. The measure of progress would be straightforward: how much time passes between a fisherman spotting an intrusion and an Indonesian agency directing an asset toward it? 
The Prabowo administration should make the North Natuna Sea the pilot for answering that question, directing its current maritime defense agencies into a single reporting chain with a common response protocol and measurable targets. Japan and Australia should focus their assistance on the communications equipment and personnel training that chain requires, while regional exercises test whether it works under operational conditions. Regional maritime domain awareness will remain incomplete until information from the first observer can reliably trigger action by the final responder.

Indonesia still faces substantial capacity limitations. In 2025, only three of the seven KKP patrol vessels assigned to the broader WPPNRI 711 area could reach the North Natuna Sea. Even when the KKP is able to catch IUU fishing boats in the act, there aren’t enough dock space or facilities to store impounded vessels and accommodate the crew. Jakarta began addressing those shortages this July by announcing ten new Class I surveillance vessels and an expansion of the PSDKP pier in Batam, which will become the principal base for operations in WPPNRI 711. 
Indonesia’s partners have likewise invested in its maritime capacity. Japan, for example, through a 9.053 billion yen grant (USD $56.57 million) is funding an offshore patrol vessel for Bakamla, scheduled for delivery in 2028. Other Japanese programs have trained Bakamla personnel in boat operations, maritime law enforcement, criminal investigations, and instructor development. Australia’s current strategic partnership plan with Indonesia provides for fisheries surveillance cooperation, maritime domain awareness information sharing, technical training, coordinated patrols, and desktop exercises. 
In early August, at the Southeast Asia Cooperation and Training exercise in Singapore, Indonesian personnel joined representatives from 15 other Indo-Pacific countries in practicing the real-time transfer of sensor data and vessel-contact information among operational centers, patrol aircraft, and ships. Days later, Bakamla hosted Malaysian and Singaporean coast guard personnel for a trilateral exercise in the Riau Islands covering cooperation in the Natuna Sea. Bakamla Chief Vice Admiral Irvansyah subsequently proposed expanding that model to other ASEAN countries. 
However, a shared regional maritime security architecture is only reliable as the national systems that feed information into it. Exchanging satellite tracks, radar data, or participating in joint exercises are meaningless if fishermen’s observations are unable to reach Indonesia’s national surveillance and enforcement system in time. 
In June, local Indonesian fishermen spotted foreign vessels conducting IUU fishing in the North Natuna Sea within Indonesia’s EEZ. The fishermen reported the sighting to patrol officers, and Indonesia’s Navy deployed the KRI John Lie-358 warship on extended patrol the following day. By the time the warship searched the area the following morning, however, the vessels had disappeared.
Government Regulation No. 13 of 2022 already provides for an integrated national maritime security and safety information system, alongside joint and coordinated patrols. Bakamla Regulation No. 2 of 2024 goes further, directing the system to improve connectivity among maritime information sources, accelerate the transmission of information about security incidents, and support more effective patrols. The legal foundation exists, but Indonesia still needs to develop a standardized operational procedure to ensure that reports reach the appropriate enforcement asset without losing critical hours along the way.
Bakamla’s command-and-control center should maintain a joint reporting and coordination process with designated liaison officers from KKP, the Indonesian Navy, the Water Police, and relevant local authorities. This center would be responsible for interagency communication and assignment, acting as a dedicated maritime desk manned through a single radio frequency and hotline for fishermen to report to. 
Jakarta should also create a Natuna-wide inventory to accurately identify key needs and distribution gaps and ensure that resources are given to those who need it most, both from a domestic perspective and as a reference point for allies when investing in resources. Capitalizing on the Prabowo administration’s recent investments in the Natuna Red and White Fishing Villages, these new hubs could act disbursement centers for communication materials while conducting training for basic vessel identification guidance and report standardization.
Indonesia’s partners should organize their assistance around this chain. Japanese-organized training could help develop watch officers and instructors capable of processing contact reports and integrating the new Bakamla vessel into joint operations. Australian information sharing and desktop exercises could test the full sequence from a fisherman’s initial report to verification and deployment. Future exercises should measure reporting, verification, and response times – not simply whether participating agencies can exchange data.
Once the system functions domestically, Indonesia can make it the foundation for regional cooperation. The next exercise with Malaysia and Singapore should begin with a simulated report from a fishing vessel, require Indonesian agencies to verify and task a response, and then test the transfer of the contact if the suspected vessel crosses into another country’s jurisdiction. Indonesia could subsequently use its position as secretariat of the 11-country Regional Plan of Action to Combat IUU Fishing to promote a common contact-report format and standardize procedures for transferring verified vessel information across borders. 
More patrol vessels will give Indonesia greater reach. They will not matter, however, if those vessels continue arriving after the target has disappeared. The measure of progress would be straightforward: how much time passes between a fisherman spotting an intrusion and an Indonesian agency directing an asset toward it?
articles.summary: Maritime security is one of Indonesia’s most demanding defense domains. And at its current stage, Indonesia needs significant help.

articles.title: Japan, South Korea, and the New Logic of Nuclear Energy Security in Northeast Asia
articles.full_text:
The two neighbors are reshaping the nuclear politics of Northeast Asia – and doing so increasingly in concert with Washington.
Japan Takahama nuclear power plant units 3 and 4.
After the 2011 accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Plant, Japan stopped all nuclear power production. Today, the country is restarting reactors, rewriting its energy law, and recasting nuclear power as a pillar of national and regional security rather than a liability to be managed. South Korea, its neighbor and rival in reactor exports, is moving along a parallel track, despite a change of government that briefly appeared to threaten the opposite. 
Together, the two countries are reshaping the nuclear politics of Northeast Asia and doing so increasingly in concert with Washington, as energy policy folds into the broader architecture of trilateral security cooperation.
The unresolved question behind both countries’ restarts is what to do with the spent fuel piling up at reactor sites. I explored one effort to solve that issue earlier this month in a visit to Japan’s Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. There, hundreds of meters below the surface, engineers are testing whether the geological disposal methods every nuclear country is counting on actually hold up over time. Horonobe is a research site, however, not a repository, and Japan still has no designated location for permanent waste disposal. That gap has not slowed the political momentum above ground.
Before 2011, nuclear power supplied roughly 30 percent of Japan’s electricity. After the meltdown at Fukushima Daiichi, every commercial reactor in the country was taken offline, and public opinion turned sharply against nuclear power. What followed was over a decade of dependence on imported liquefied natural gas and coal, at a cost Japan, which imports about 90 percent of its primary energy, could not sustain indefinitely, especially as global gas markets tightened after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The return to nuclear power began in earnest with Prime Minister Kishida Fumio’s Green Transformation (GX) policy, launched in 2022. The GX Basic Policy, approved by the Cabinet in February 2023, explicitly committed the government to restarting reactors already cleared by regulators and to building next-generation designs. 
The Seventh Strategic Energy Plan, approved by the Cabinet in February 2025 along with the accompanying GX2040 Vision, cemented nuclear power’s return as government policy rather than a temporary emergency measure. In early 2026, that policy produced its most tangible result yet: the restart of Unit 6 at Tokyo Electric Power Company’s Kashiwazaki-Kariwa plant, the world’s largest nuclear facility by capacity. Perhaps more pointedly, it’s run by the operator directly responsible for Fukushima Daiichi. Such a restart would have been politically unthinkable a decade ago.
The motivation is obvious. New public funding for data center and semiconductor facilities, worth over a trillion yen, requires that the electricity used come entirely from renewable or nuclear sources. That sends an unambiguous signal that Tokyo now considers nuclear energy to be indispensable to industrial policy, not just decarbonization.
South Korea is moving along a similar trajectory, even if it once looked to be headed in a different direction. President Lee Jae-myung took office in June 2025 after having campaigned on skepticism toward nuclear power. Lee argued that the technology was inherently dangerous and that the country’s reactor-heavy generation mix needed re-examining in favor of renewables. Seven months later, confronted with polling showing strong public support for nuclear energy and with surging electricity demand from an AI-driven data center boom, his government reversed course.
Seoul confirmed it would proceed with two new large reactors under the 11th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand, which targets a nuclear share of nearly 32 percent by 2030 and over 35 percent by 2038. In August 2026, Lee’s government went further, naming small modular reactors and nuclear fusion among seven technologies it wants to establish as future growth engines for the South Korean economy.
Korean reactor technology is already competitive with Western vendors. Around the same time Lee took office, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power signed a contract to build two APR-1000 reactors in Dukovany, Czechia, a deal worth roughly $18.6 billion. The company has since signed cooperation agreements covering nuclear development in the Philippines, small-reactors studies with Singapore, and full fuel-cycle cooperation with France’s Orano. South Korea, which imports roughly 90 percent of its own energy needs and around 30 percent of its low-enriched uranium from Russia, is treating nuclear exports and domestic energy security as two sides of the same policy.
In July 2026, nuclear energy became an area of interest for trilateral cooperation between the United States and its two East Asian Allies. Japan, South Korea, and the United States agreed to jointly develop and export small modular reactors across the Indo-Pacific, explicitly extending their trilateral security partnership into commercial nuclear cooperation. 
With Russia and China as the only realistic nuclear vendors for many developing countries, Washington has a clear interest in ensuring that Japan and South Korea enter the race. It would benefit Washington if its two Northeast Asian allies, rather than Beijing or Moscow, become the default suppliers of reactor technology to the rest of the region. 
For Tokyo and Seoul, folding nuclear commerce into the trilateral security relationship also offers insurance against the awkward fact that both countries’ export ambitions still run through Washington’s non-proliferation rules and, in South Korea’s case, the 123 Agreement governing nuclear cooperation with the United States.
Japan’s own export potential remains constrained precisely because its domestic restart is still incomplete. Barely a handful of reactors are back online out of the roughly three dozen that existed before 2011. That leaves South Korea, for now, as the more credible reactor exporter of the two. 
What the restart narrative tends to leave out is that neither country has solved the problem I found researchers still puzzling over at Horonobe: Japan has no operating deep geological repository and no site formally designated to host one. That means the used fuel accumulating at reactor sites, including at the restarted Kashiwazaki-Kariwa plant, has nowhere permanent to go. South Korea faces the same problem, with domestic opposition to any proposed storage site consistently more intense than opposition to reactors themselves.
That gap matters for the trilateral SMR push, too. Exporting reactor technology to Southeast Asia or the Pacific Islands without a credible regional answer on waste management invites the same criticism that has dogged nuclear power at home in both countries: that the industry is better at building political consensus for new construction than for dealing with what construction leaves behind. 
For now, Northeast Asia’s nuclear revival is a story about energy security, industrial competitiveness, and alignment with Washington against Chinese and Russian reactor diplomacy. But underneath all these developments lurks the unanswered question of what to do with the increasing amounts of nuclear waste. That may end up mattering as much to the region’s energy future as any restart or export deal announced so far.

articles.title: Ayesha Siddiqa on the Pakistan Army’s Police State
articles.full_text:
Siddiqa argues that Pakistan is not a hybrid regime but a case of constitutional militarism, sanctioned by a parliament that has legislated away its own relevance.
Dr. Ayesha Siddiqa, senior fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and author of “Military Inc.,” joins host Tushar Shetty to examine the Pakistan Army’s role in the country’s governance. 
They discuss the origins of the military’s dominance in the years after 1947, its influence over domestic politics and the economy, its conduct of foreign policy from Ayub Khan to Asim Munir, and its handling of the insurgencies in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Siddiqa argues that Pakistan is not a hybrid regime but a case of constitutional militarism, sanctioned by a parliament that has legislated away its own relevance. 
For more in-depth analysis on South Asia, subscribe to the Beyond the Indus podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts, or follow us on YouTube for video episodes.

articles.title: Jeremy Douglas on Southeast Asia’s Drug Boom
articles.full_text:
“This is a region that is arguably now the largest epicenter of synthetic drug production in the world,” says the UNDOC deputy director.
A panoramic view of the Golden Triangle confluence, where the borders of Myanmar, Thailand, and Laos converge
Late last month, Indonesian authorities announced the seizure of around 2.6 tons of liquid methamphetamine from a ship off the coast of Sumatra. The bust was just the latest in a series of drug mega-seizures that have taken place over the past two years, as the region’s law enforcement agencies struggle to combat an unprecedented surge in trafficking.
According to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), authorities in East and Southeast Asia seized a record 349 tons of methamphetamine in 2025, a 48 percent increase over the previous year – and just 65 tons a decade ago. Seizures of ketamine also hit 52 tons, up 185 percent on 2024.
What lies behind Asia’s drug boom? The Diplomat’s Southeast Asia Editor Sebastian Strangio spoke recently with Jeremy Douglas, deputy director of operations at the UNODC, who previously spent a decade as the agency’s lead for East and Southeast Asia in Bangkok. Douglas spoke about the factors that have contributed to the unprecedented levels of drug production, the impact of civil war in Myanmar, and what might be done to stem the tide of illegal narcotics. Watch the interview, or keep scrolling for the transcript.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
First, why don’t you give us an overview of the issue in terms of particularly synthetic drug production? What are the basic trend lines and what is the current scale of the crisis?
Well, the trend is not good. We have a region that last year sees 350 tons of crystal methamphetamine [of seizures], 50 tons of ketamine. This is a region that is arguably now the largest epicenter of synthetic drug production in the world. If you look at what is seized in the region, 90 percent of it I’m guessing at the moment is seized in the Mekong. So within Southeast Asia, if you look at the concentration point of the Mekong and within that the upper Mekong, that’s where the vast majority is seized.
That concentration point is exceeding North America. And possibly Myanmar is now the largest source in the world. So the trend is that it’s just going up, up, up and there’s no brake on the production at all. It’s diversifying, as I said, ketamine has come onto the scene in a big way, 50 tons last year. There’s no other part of the world that’s seizing ketamine on that scale. So it’s really a bad trend line, and we don’t see this reversing anytime soon.
Most of this drug production takes place in what is known as the Golden Triangle, the tri-border area between Myanmar, Laos, and Thailand. Now this is a region that’s historically been associated with opium and heroin production going right back through the Cold War and even to colonial times. What underpinned the shift to synthetic drugs such as methamphetamine and ketamine in recent years? When did this shift begin?
Well, methamphetamine started really being produced in a big way in in the early 2000s in in the Golden Triangle – in Shan State, just north of that tri-border area you just referred to. And it was a form called yaba. And yaba was very localized. So, it was produced for the Thai market primarily, used by workers, factory workers, taxi drivers, truck drivers, and so on and so forth, right?
So that was the first wave. But yaba is a cheap form of methamphetamine. You don’t find it in other parts of the world, except that Mekong subregion and really in Thailand. So it’s a unique product. I worked there 2002 to 2007, and that’s when we really saw it flooding out and we were studying and tracking the trends and the locations from where it was coming and so forth at that time.
At that time though, it was still a huge production point for opium and heroin, which is coming out and reaching markets as far as Australia, in some cases even to Europe or California – you’d see Golden Triangle heroin reaching far. In and around 2010, we saw the expansion of methamphetamine across Southeast Asia, but at that time production was kind of scattered. It was in South China primarily, in big industrial production areas [like] Guangdong, in the Philippines, in Indonesia, crystal meth I’m referring to at this point. So again, yaba stays concentrated in the in the Mekong. Crystal meth is being produced in the other parts of Southeast Asia.
In and around 2010, when that’s you start seeing a little bit of crystal meth coming out of Myanmar, out of Shan State. Not very much, a little bit. In 2013-14, you start seeing more, but it’s really not in a big, big way. And then in 2015, something happens, and that’s an event in Lufeng in China. Now at that point we had a lot of crystal meth from that particular location I’m referring to, Guangdong – Lufeng is in Guangdong – spilling out. But China had a very aggressive anti-drugs campaign, in part under pressure from Australia and other countries. They were working closely together to go after methamphetamine trafficking. Intelligence was being shared. Anyway, there’s this meth village Lufeng, a very famous operation to take out methamphetamine labs there. They essentially crushed it.
But that actually caused a displacement effect. So right after that, we suddenly start seeing crystal meth rising out of the Golden Triangle. What had occurred was the organized crime syndicates that were sourcing out of Guangdong said, okay, we can go back to what we used to where we used to source our heroin. And this is some very sophisticated organized crime groups that had decided to synthetic take the market into the direction of synthetic. So they shifted their production, they made investments in labs with ethnic armed groups and other groups inside Myanmar. They shifted their production there and then that’s what we see today.
That’s not to say that heroin is not still a concern. We still see it. It started rising, particularly post-coup [in Myanmar] where we see people returning to make an income. You know, the economy tanked in Myanmar. So people went back to into opium production. So now we see more and more heroin, but not now nowhere on the scale that we did in in the mid-2000s, early 2000s.
Let’s talk a bit more about who’s actually responsible for this production. Is it predominantly Chinese criminal syndicates that have moved into Myanmar, or are there other criminal groups that are involved as well?
Well, it was actually some major ethnic Chinese organized crime groups, triads, some people refer to them as triads, those are very old in the region, right? So we’ve had the heroin trafficking you referred to earlier, which spilled out in colonial times or in the Cold War era. the triads would go and source heroin. So those groups have long, long ties in the region. And they have bases. They operate in Bangkok, they operate in Malaysia, they operate in Jakarta. But of course they’re primarily centered in South China, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan.
So those are the groups that partnered with the armed groups in Myanmar and shifted that production in. Within those groups, there’s a kind of famous case, a gentleman named Tse Chi Lop. He was arguably the man who really revolutionized the business with his syndicate, Sam Gor syndicate. They partnered up very effectively with armed groups in in Shan to source meth, to invest in those labs that I was referring to before. That group was, I would argue, the biggest of the ones and behind a lot of what I’ve described: the teabag meth.
Myanmar had a military coup in 2021, which was followed by protests and then an armed uprising that inflamed the existing conflicts in the country, particularly its ethnic conflicts. What impact has that had on the political economy of Shan State and of the drug industry in that part of Myanmar?
It’s had a phenomenal impact. As I said earlier, just talking about opium, opium for poor people is a way to have an income. And when the economy tanked post-coup, you saw a lot of people lose their jobs in Mandalay, lose them in Yangon, lose them in towns. They returned to their villages, they don’t have other sources of income, there’s less cash flowing in society. So they return to what they know. And so we see people returning to opium farming at that point looking for an income. So that’s a direct, very clear impact. You can see the trend line right after the coup.
Synthetics are slightly different. They’re not an employer as such, because a very small, tight knit organized crime group or armed group working with organized crime can produce mass amounts with a lab and a small group of specialists, chemists and others. But that is coming from the same kind of geography as the opium: very remote, no rule of law, no state authority. So essentially that there was no brake on the synthetics being produced in there because there was no functional government paying attention to the drug trade because they were preoccupied with fighting insurgency or fighting back against the different various movements that were fighting them.
So on the one hand, you have the poverty-induced production of opium. On the other, you have no brake and nobody stepping in to try to stop the precursors flowing in and the drugs flowing out on the synthetic side. So it’s really an explosion at that point. And now we see what we saw last year, this 350 tons of meth being seized. That’s a fraction of what’s actually produced seized in in the region. So it’s just phenomenal.
Another development that’s been alarming in this region in recent years has been the rise of online scamming, particularly these industrial scale scamming compounds which have been established across Cambodia, Laos, but also in parts of Myanmar that are home to most drug production. To what extent are these two criminal ecosystems interwoven or connected?
Well, the scam ecosystem has evolved fast. It’s come on fast, it’s also evolved very quickly in a very short period of time, but at least the early stages of it were very, very deeply connected to the drug trade in an interesting way. In and around the time I referred to, 2015, when you see that flood of crystal, the profits being generated by the drug trade grow exponentially and business people –organized crime figures are also business people – they start looking for places to invest their money. They need places to launder their money. So there’s this explosion of casinos that takes place inside Southeast Asia. You see it in the Golden Triangle, the special economic zone there. You see it also up in the special regions up in northern Myanmar. You see this along the Thai border, Tachileik and different locations, Cambodia, casinos everywhere.
Now, that casino model that they had, they can launder money through those things. A lot of them had drug and drug money investors in the casino infrastructure. But then that also gave them a vehicle through which they could facilitate payments through junkets and the casinos themselves to those that they needed to pay in the drug business. The casinos were serving as that vehicle.
Then COVID hits. And what happens to the casinos? They lose their foot traffic, which is tourists, mainly from mainland China, but also from the region itself, that were walking in and creating “legitimate” business. That COVID hit stops the foot traffic. But they still had a lot of money, so basically put the casinos online. They become online gaming companies.
So we saw suddenly online games popping up all over Southeast Asia. The same infrastructure in many locations has served as scam infrastructure. So that’s the beginning connection and the strongest connection still to this day. And a lot of the guys that were laundering the drug money in the region went straight into taking money that they made from the drugs, taking the money they made from the casinos, and reinvesting it in new business lines, scams, using the IT infrastructure that they had built for themselves when the casinos went online during the COVID era.
Now of course now scams have taken off in a different direction. All kinds of people came in with their own ideas and you’ve got technology involved and there’s non-drug people involved as well. So it’s not just drug money, but nonetheless there’s that deep connection.
Right. Now, looking at some of the recent UNODC reports, they really stress the idea that these syndicates are innovators. They’re constantly thinking and anticipating law enforcement operations and they’ve become quite adept at changing things up in response to official crackdowns. What sorts of methods are they now using in terms of both production and trafficking to try and evade these efforts?
articles.summary: "This is a region that is arguably now the largest epicenter of synthetic drug production in the world," says the UNDOC deputy director.

articles.title: China Wants to Push Taiwan out of the Pacific
articles.full_text:
China’s pressure campaign against Taiwan doesn’t end when a country switches recognition to Beijing.
Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung during a visit to Palau to attend the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ Meeting, Aug. 27, 2026.
Taiwan and China are back at the annual Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders Meeting, returning after all external partners were excluded in 2025. And Beijing isn’t happy about it: China’s special envoy called Taiwan’s participation “very inappropriate” and warned, “There will always be consequences.”
With multiple Pacific leaders not in attendance amid whispers of foreign interference, China-Taiwan competition is on everyone’s minds. While no Pacific country switched recognition in 2026, Beijing’s pressure campaign this year has been more systematic and intense than in any year since Naoero (formerly Nauru) flipped ties in 2024.
Under Beijing’s version of the “One China” principle – which holds that Taiwan is part of China – limiting Taiwan’s international space is an ever-present imperative. For Taiwan, defending its sovereignty entails maintaining, and where possible, expanding its diplomatic presence. 
Competition across the Taiwan Strait is clearest to outside observers when countries switch recognition from Taiwan to China, yet for Beijing it never ends there. China then wants to win repeated rhetorical affirmation of the One China principle, institutional buy-in beyond the government of the day, and concrete decisions to limit Taiwan’s presence.
Across the nine Pacific countries where China has diplomatic missions, officials re-affirm their support for Beijing’s One China principle in roughly one in three publicized meetings with Chinese diplomats, according to The Alliance Futures Initiative’s PRC Pacific Embassies Monitor. That rate reflects China’s embassies’ frequent maintenance work aimed at ensuring incumbent and incoming officials are reminded of their support for One China principle. 
Beyond government officials, China also engages with political parties to secure their institutional backing. In July 2026, a delegation of the People’s Alliance Party of Fiji met with the International Liaison Department (ILD) – the Chinese apparatus for party-party relations – in China, giving its institutional support for the One China principle. Later that month, an ILD delegation met with parties across the Solomon Islands political spectrum. 
These statements carry real weight. Just days before the PIF Leaders’ Meeting, Vanuatu’s opposition leader called on the government to affirm its support for the One China principle. The opposition also urged the government to ensure its actions at the upcoming forum will be consistent with the One China principle. In other words: don’t engage with Taiwan. The government responded by rejecting the opposition’s concerns and affirming its adherence to the One China principle. The opposition party’s call shows how Beijing’s drive for support ultimately leads to Pacific governments taking concrete decisions that shrink Taiwan’s international space.
The most tangible recent case was Papua New Guinea’s decision to close Taiwan’s trade office in its capital this July. Prime Minister James Marape rejected claims of foreign pressure, stating that the decision reflected PNG’s longstanding One China policy, which recognizes Beijing’s assertion of sovereignty across the Taiwan Strait. Taipei responded by suspending spot purchases of liquefied natural gas, yet by keeping long-term contracts preserved some of its presence.
Richard Maru, PNG’s trade and international investment minister, has publicly tied Chinese economic benefits to PNG’s moves against Taiwan. In May 2026, Maru attributed a recently signed economic framework agreement in part to the 2023 closure of PNG’s trade office in Taipei.
The closure of Taiwan’s trade office also followed Marape’s April 2026 visit to China, which focused on expanding trade and investment ties with Guangdong. The week before the closure, Maru met with the Chinese ambassador to discuss the upcoming inaugural PNG-China Business Forum & Trade Expo and other economic matters.
China didn’t need to ask PNG to oust Taiwan; it had already made it clear that PNG would be rewarded for it. 
Following the closure, China’s ambassador to PNG, Yang Xiaoguang, published an article in the local press titled “Closing Down the ‘Taipei Economic Office in PNG’ Will Further Enhance China-PNG Relations and Cooperation.” Sure enough, a PetroChina delegation arrived in Port Moresby days after the closure with offers to buy more PNG gas.
China amplified these developments across the Pacific, with embassies uniformly featuring the closure on their social media. In the Federated States of Micronesia and Fiji, China’s heads of mission published opinion pieces in the local media about the importance of following Beijing’s version of the One China principle, with the PNG move as the highlight.
China’s chargé d’affaires in Fiji, Wang Yuan, used his editorial as a platform to remind his hosts of their next step to align with China’s One China principle. Wang opened by emphasizing the importance of adherence to the One China principle to the China-Fiji relationship, then  went on to celebrate PNG closing the trade office. He commended Fiji for closing its trade office in Taiwan back in 2017 and renaming and revoking diplomatic privileges for Taiwan’s office in Suva in 2019. 
Wang didn’t explicitly ask Fiji to close the Taipei Trade Office. He didn’t need to. The sequence made it obvious what Beijing would like to see next – and by publishing an editorial, Wang put the idea in front of Fiji’s government and public at the same time.
Other governments in the region have also taken steps to shore up the strength of their support for Beijing’s One China principle. In May 2026, Naoero’s Cabinet issued a directive to all government and state-owned enterprise employees to firmly adhere to the One China principle and ensure consistency with it in official practices and communications. The directive also proscribed all official engagements with what it calls “Taiwan Province.”
In Kiribati, President Taneti Maamau just argued for a proposed constitutional amendment that would limit diplomatic relations to only U.N. member countries. In effect, the bill would prevent Kiribati from re-establishing ties with Taiwan. Regardless of whether the amendment passes, the bill aims to bind future officials to Beijing’s preferences. With the timing just days before the PIF Leaders’ Meeting in Palau – a country that recognizes Taiwan – the move suggested the weight Beijing carries in Kiribati, a country that only switched ties itself in 2019.
As these cases show, Beijing’s work to shrink Taiwan’s international space doesn’t end with recognition. After a country first gives its support for Beijing’s One China principle, China continues to expect increasing adherence. By rewarding anti-Taiwan actions, China signals that others will be paid too. 
Taiwan, Washington, and their partners are asking the wrong question. Which country flips next is less important than which piece of Taiwan’s presence will disappear next.
Taiwan and China are back at the annual Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders Meeting, returning after all external partners were excluded in 2025. And Beijing isn’t happy about it: China’s special envoy called Taiwan’s participation “very inappropriate” and warned, “There will always be consequences.”
With multiple Pacific leaders not in attendance amid whispers of foreign interference, China-Taiwan competition is on everyone’s minds. While no Pacific country switched recognition in 2026, Beijing’s pressure campaign this year has been more systematic and intense than in any year since Naoero (formerly Nauru) flipped ties in 2024.
Under Beijing’s version of the “One China” principle – which holds that Taiwan is part of China – limiting Taiwan’s international space is an ever-present imperative. For Taiwan, defending its sovereignty entails maintaining, and where possible, expanding its diplomatic presence. 
Competition across the Taiwan Strait is clearest to outside observers when countries switch recognition from Taiwan to China, yet for Beijing it never ends there. China then wants to win repeated rhetorical affirmation of the One China principle, institutional buy-in beyond the government of the day, and concrete decisions to limit Taiwan’s presence.
Across the nine Pacific countries where China has diplomatic missions, officials re-affirm their support for Beijing’s One China principle in roughly one in three publicized meetings with Chinese diplomats, according to The Alliance Futures Initiative’s PRC Pacific Embassies Monitor. That rate reflects China’s embassies’ frequent maintenance work aimed at ensuring incumbent and incoming officials are reminded of their support for One China principle. 
Beyond government officials, China also engages with political parties to secure their institutional backing. In July 2026, a delegation of the People’s Alliance Party of Fiji met with the International Liaison Department (ILD) – the Chinese apparatus for party-party relations – in China, giving its institutional support for the One China principle. Later that month, an ILD delegation met with parties across the Solomon Islands political spectrum. 
These statements carry real weight. Just days before the PIF Leaders’ Meeting, Vanuatu’s opposition leader called on the government to affirm its support for the One China principle. The opposition also urged the government to ensure its actions at the upcoming forum will be consistent with the One China principle. In other words: don’t engage with Taiwan. The government responded by rejecting the opposition’s concerns and affirming its adherence to the One China principle. The opposition party’s call shows how Beijing’s drive for support ultimately leads to Pacific governments taking concrete decisions that shrink Taiwan’s international space.
The most tangible recent case was Papua New Guinea’s decision to close Taiwan’s trade office in its capital this July. Prime Minister James Marape rejected claims of foreign pressure, stating that the decision reflected PNG’s longstanding One China policy, which recognizes Beijing’s assertion of sovereignty across the Taiwan Strait. Taipei responded by suspending spot purchases of liquefied natural gas, yet by keeping long-term contracts preserved some of its presence.
Richard Maru, PNG’s trade and international investment minister, has publicly tied Chinese economic benefits to PNG’s moves against Taiwan. In May 2026, Maru attributed a recently signed economic framework agreement in part to the 2023 closure of PNG’s trade office in Taipei.
articles.summary: China’s pressure campaign against Taiwan doesn’t end when a country switches recognition to Beijing.

articles.title: Tajikistan Taxes Tourism Trips Abroad to Fund Development at Home
articles.full_text:
The new rules would hit Tajikistan’s tourism companies while benefiting an affiliated state body.
Tajikistan has created a Tourism Development Fund financed in part by a payment of 5 percent of the sale value of tour packages sold to Tajik citizens travelling abroad. The resolution was adopted on July 1 but publicized only in late August.
The new rules open a dedicated account at the Ministry of Finance’s Central Treasury. Listed sources also include a per-day charge on foreign visitors’ packages, permit fees, fines, deposit income, and grants from international financial institutions. Spending is authorized by a 13-member council chaired by the head of the Committee for Tourism Development, alongside deputy ministers, agency heads, and one private sector representative.
For inbound visitors the charge is negligible: 0.2 of the annual calculation indicator per 24-hour period in hotels and 0.15 in guesthouses, or 15.6 and 11.7 somoni ($1.70 and $1.30) at the 2026 indicator of 78 somoni. The outbound payment is where the revenue is, and it reaches most of the tourism industry. Of 191 registered tourism companies, the committee counts 75 to 84 in inbound work and only around 30 active companies. Most of the remainder primarily arrange trips abroad for Tajik citizens.
Because the payment is calculated on the package’s sale price rather than the tourism agency’s commission, the tax is imposed on the transaction’s gross value, not the agency’s margin. On an illustrative 20,000 somoni package the payment is 1,000 somoni, roughly a third of the 3,194 somoni average monthly wage reported in June. Sellers will either absorb that fee, raise prices, or restructure sales. 
“We haven’t done final math on the implications of this new tax for us, but it is not a development we’re happy about,” the head of a well-established Dushanbe-based tourism company told The Diplomat on condition of anonymity. “Our margins are thin as it is and now we might have to rethink our entire business model.”
On the published wording the payment targets packages sold by tourism companies. If separately booked flights, hotel rooms, and insurance fall outside the definition of a taxable package, the rules could create an incentive to unbundle trips or shift bookings to foreign platforms, disadvantaging licensed Tajik tourism companies and leaving them with compliance burden.
The rules do build in safeguards – the council reviews targeted use of funds and audit reports, the committee reports to the government twice a year, and annual activity information is to be published. But the council is chaired by the head of the agency whose staff also serve as its secretariat and disclosure is annual rather than transaction-level. The rules specify only one private-sector representative and do not identify an independent civil-society or external oversight member. 
Asia-Plus reported that 30 percent of monthly receipts will be transferred automatically to an “Information Center of Tourism Services” for operational measures and incentives for sector employees, with no stated allocation criteria.
Kazakhstan’s outbound tourism mechanism creates a direct traveler entitlement: Kazakh operators pay into Turistik Qamqor, a fund whose stated sole purpose is returning Kazakh travelers home when an operator fails, with each traveler issued a code that triggers the guarantee. Tajikistan’s rules set out no equivalent right for travelers.
The fund arrives as the government is highlighting both growth and strain. Tajikistan recorded 1.063 million foreign entrants in the first half of 2026, of whom 889,400 were classified as foreign tourists (a narrower category than total foreign entries), up 16.7 percent. Committee Chairman Jamshed Jurakhonzoda has said border crossings cannot absorb the flow, sanitation along the main highways is poor, mobile coverage fails in the mountains, and trained guides are scarce. 
The government has already committed more than 270 million somoni to its 2027-2030 tourism strategy. Of that earmarked amount, 60.9 million (or 22 percent) comes from the state budget, a quarter is provided by development partners and international institutions, and 143.6 million or over half is expected from the private sector. No revenue estimate has been published for the new levy, which will be drawn largely from Tajiks buying their way out of the country where the government is simultaneously asking private tourism businesses to finance more than half of its next tourism strategy.

articles.title: Was Abe Shinzo an Idealist?
articles.full_text:
A new biography of Japan’s longest-serving prime minister reevaluates his realist legacy.
Then-Prime Minister Abe Shinzo delivers a policy speech on Oct. 4, 2019.
In Japan, books written about Abe Shinzo, the country’s longest-serving prime minister, have become an industry unto themselves. However, most of them tend to reflect a partisan bias – perhaps fitting for such a controversial political figure, who once described himself as a “fighting politician.” At worst, his detractors have portrayed him as a would-be dictator, while his devotees have cast him as a messianic figure. More analytical assessments, meanwhile, have earned his foreign policy a strong reputation as pragmatic and realistic.
Yet, until recently, no full-length biography of Abe had been published, partly for the obvious reason that his death came so suddenly. The closest thing to a biographical study was Tobias Harris’ “The Iconoclast,” published in 2020. That has now changed. A more comprehensive biography on Abe by Hattori Ryuji, professor of Chuo University, was just released by Chuo Koron Shinsha.
Hattori’s short but detailed biography of Abe Shinzo could be regarded as a revisionist work in its own right, challenging the conventional wisdom – one that has also gained international currency – that Abe can be strictly characterized as a realist foreign policy thinker. Written by a diplomatic historian, the book focuses extensively on the foreign policy decisions made during Abe’s tenure as prime minister, drawing on newly declassified diplomatic documents that the author was able to access. Hattori’s conclusion is that, while Abe possessed a “remarkable strategic vision,” he was ultimately “an imperfect realist.”
Abe’s visionary thinking was an outlier in a country whose postwar prime ministers – almost all of them from the Liberal Democratic Party – were generally known for their conciliatory approach and skill in building intraparty coalitions. They were politicians more accustomed to working behind the scenes than articulating bold visions in public. 
Among Abe’s many foreign policy conceptions, the most famous was the “Free and Open Indo-Pacific,” a strategic vision that not only articulated Japan’s broader interests in the world but also encouraged other governments to adapt to a new century in which the influence and potential of the Indo-Pacific region had become greater than ever before. 
One of the clearest examples of the practical implementation of this vision was Abe’s promotion of free trade. His administration played a crucial role in bringing the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) to fruition after the United States withdrew from the original TPP, while also advancing the Japan-EU Economic Partnership Agreement and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) negotiations.
However, while Abe’s vision of maintaining a liberal international order fostered a strong affinity with the West, his misconceptions and even biases may have constrained his ability to pursue constructive diplomacy in East Asia. This, in turn, highlights the imperfect side of Abe’s realism. According to Hattori’s account, Abe’s eagerness to reach deals with Russia and China may have led him to surrender valuable leverage – and, perhaps more importantly, some of the legitimacy underpinning Japan’s position on the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China claims as the Diaoyu. In negotiations with Beijing, this resulted in a memorandum that could be interpreted as acknowledging that a territorial dispute existed, even though Japan’s official position has long been that no such dispute exists. 
Abe also failed to achieve a breakthrough in his foreign policy toward the Korean Peninsula. He built a reputation as a champion of the Japanese citizens who had been abducted by North Korea. Yet he was ultimately unable to translate his hardline stance into a successful diplomatic strategy, nor was he willing to resort to inducements – the road not taken. 
Also, vis-à-vis South Korea, Abe never developed a genuine rapport with any of his counterparts, unlike some of his successors. His determination not to give an inch on historical controversies constrained his ability to compromise, plunging bilateral relations into their worst state since the normalization of diplomatic ties. Nevertheless, when Abe did in fact cede ground – as in the agreement with South Korea that acknowledged Japan’s remorse over the “comfort women” while framing the settlement of the issue as “final and irreversible” – his failure to follow through on the resulting rapprochement allowed the issue to resurface once there was a change in government in Seoul.
The apparent failure of Abe’s East Asian diplomacy is all the more remarkable given the influence of his grandfather, Kishi Nobusuke. Kishi instilled in his grandson a mission to right the wrongs of the U.S. occupation – most notably, by revising the pacifist Constitution – as well as a commitment to a strong alliance with the United States, which Kishi himself helped lay the foundation for by revising the security treaty on more equal terms.
Although Kishi was said to have been influenced by Pan-Asianism and understood the importance of maintaining good relations with Japan’s neighboring countries, the premium he placed on Asian diplomacy was not inherited by his grandson. In fact, Abe seemed emotionally incapable of identifying Japan with the East rather than the West. This sentiment was manifested in a book he co-authored in 1996, when he was still a rising young conservative. The book warned: “Such an excessive attachment to the idea that ‘we are a part of Asia’ can become a dangerous spark that, from a policy perspective, risks triggering fatal mistakes.”
To understand the limits of Abe’s realism, it is necessary to identify the factors that prevented him from fully realizing the realist ideal. These included his historical perceptions, his strong concern with his political legacy, and his sense of duty and personal sentiment. Taken together, these characteristics suggest that Abe may be better understood as an idealist in the broader sense: a political actor who sought to translate deeply held beliefs and principles into political reality, regardless of the distance between his ideals and the circumstances he faced.
Hattori himself does not characterize Abe as an idealist. Nevertheless, his contribution in questioning the realist label so often attached to Abe as a foreign policy strategist represents a meaningful starting point for a more clear-eyed and constructive discussion of a politician who continues to evoke considerable passion and controversy. 
More pages will be written about Abe, both domestically and abroad, in the years ahead. And with every page turned, the present will see how much of a mark he left on Japan.
