articles.title: Taiwan Finally Passed Its 2026 Budget. What Got Cut?
articles.full_text:
The budget was passed almost 9 months late, amid growing concern that defense spending was being held up – especially funding for drones.
After many months of contention over Taiwan’s government spending, the pan-Blue camp seemed to finally relent on August 14. The budget was finally passed on that day – 266 days past the deadline, and almost one year after the Executive Yuan originally submitted the budget for consideration on August 29, 2025.
The eventual passage of the budget occurred amid growing concern that defense spending was being held up – especially funding for drones. 
The Kuomintang (KMT) – which currently holds the majority in the legislature along with its third-party ally, the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) – had previously suggested that it would cut funding or impose funding freezes on drone spending, alleging that the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) was using the drone industry to funnel money to untested companies and line its pockets. Reports at the time in pan-Green media outlets also suggested that China hoped to see drone spending blocked and had directed United Front Work Departments to coordinate to influence public opinion in Taiwan. 
However, the KMT seemed to suddenly reverse course after an article in The Economist accused the party of failing to protect Taiwan’s democracy out of the political selfishness of its politicians.
Still, the budget that was passed had substantial cuts, including with regard to drone spending. The cuts amounted to 1.7 percent of the Executive Yuan’s original budget, which KMT legislative caucus leader Fu Kun-chi framed as a generous gesture. By comparison, in 2025, when the KMT instituted the largest set of budget cuts in Taiwanese political history – freezing or cutting one-third of the government’s operational expenses – this was around 3 percent of the proposed budget. 
When it comes to drone funding, the Lai administration originally intended to pass a special budget of NT$210 billion (US$6.6 billion) that would have been used to purchase 1,446 coastal reconnaissance drones, 208,200 coastal attack drones, and 1,320 unmanned surface vessels. The budget would have run from August 2026 through the end of 2031, with spending of NT$42.1 billion per year. Importantly, that would have come on top of NT$31 billion budgeted by the military for unmanned systems as part of its existing budget. 
The budget passed by the KMT allocated NT$240 billion in funding for all purchases of unmanned systems, which will be under the budget for the central government rather than as a separate special budget. Spending would be limited to a cap of NT$40 billion per year, which would be subject to regulatory approval. In other words, the KMT has reduced the budget for military spending on drones from around NT$73 billion a year to NT$40 billion – a 45 percent reduction.
The KMT intends to exert control over the process for drone development through annual approval. Industry experts have warned that this could be detrimental for the long-term development of Taiwan’s drone industry. Building up domestic drone capacity usually requires an initial injection of capital that then tapers off, rather than the same amount of funding year after year. Likewise, drone companies will have to face uncertainty, as the KMT could deny approval for funding in subsequent cycles. 
Some reports suggest that the Executive Yuan will accept the reduced drone budget nonetheless, although it is possible that it may still attempt to fight for additional funding. 
The KMT has sought to deny funding to defense initiatives undertaken by the Tsai and Lai administrations, claiming that effectiveness has not yet been proven. Beyond drones, under the current budget, the KMT has moved to freeze NT$11.9 billion in funding for Taiwan’s domestic submarine program – for the completion of a planned fleet of seven submarines – until after testing for the first submarine of the fleet, the Hai Kun. 
Besides defense programs, the new budget brings other cuts. All media and publicity budgets were slashed by half, while all special operational expenses were but by 60 percent. It is expected that cuts to media and publicity budgets will impact the ability of the government to advertise social services, conduct outreach about civil resilience, and even recruit soldiers. 
A number of key ministries will see special operational expenses slashed to zero. This includes the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of National Defense, Ministry of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Transportation and Communication, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Labor, Ministry of Digital Affairs, and Ministry of Culture. Likewise, the National Development Council, National Communications Commission, Mainland Affairs Council, Overseas Community Affairs Council, Ocean Affairs Council, and Ministry of Personnel will also have special operational expenses reduced to zero. 
Funding for international exchanges has proven to be another target. Overseas travel and foreign training budgets were cut by 70 percent for the National Development Council, National Communications Commission, Mainland Affairs Council (MAC), Overseas Community Affairs Council, and the Control Yuan. Such funding was cut by 10 percent for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of National Defense, National Security Council, National Science and Technology Council, National Police Agency, National Fire Agency, Ministry of Sports, National Immigration Agency, and Coast Guard Administration.
The Ministry of Culture has seen its budget cut by NT$1 billion and NT$386 million is frozen. Another NT$21.85 million was cut, and NT$300 million was frozen for Public Television Services, which includes English-language Taiwan Plus. The National Communications Commission, whose operation is already frozen because the KMT refuses to confirm new nominees to it, will see a 56 percent funding cut. The oversight body of the Control Yuan, which includes the National Human Rights Commission, will see NT$295 million in cuts. 
Some cuts target specific politicians that the KMT dislikes. President Lai Ching-te has seen his annual discretionary budget of NT$30 million cut by one-third to NT$20 million, the remainder of which was then frozen. The annual discretionary budget is usually used for disaster relief funding. Premier Cho Jung-tai has also had his salary frozen for September to December 2026. 
With its discretionary funding frozen, the Presidential Office stated that it had to cancel mooncake orders from organizations that hold workshops for individuals with intellectual disabilities. That lead to criticisms from Taichung mayor Lu Shiow-yen of the KMT, who claimed that the Presidential Office was attempting to manipulate public opinion through canceling the orders. Lu said that the Taichung mayoral administration would step in to pay for the mooncakes. Later on, KMT legislative caucus leader Fu Kun-chi apologized and stated that the legislature would cover the cost. 
It seems that large-scale budget cuts are par for the course with the KMT in control of the legislature. The KMT clearly intends to throw a wrench into initiatives of the Lai administration through cuts or freezes. While the KMT’s budget cuts provoked significant outrage last year in the form of the Great Recall Movement – the historic but ultimately unsuccessful attempt to recall all KMT legislators – any anger this year is likely to be channeled toward local elections in November. That being said, the local elections are for positions such as mayor and city/county councilors and will not impact the composition of the legislature. The results will not have any direct impact on future budgeting decisions by the Legislative Yuan. 
It is to be seen if there are similar delays in passing the budget next year. The Executive Yuan submitted its 2027 budget on August 19. With more than NT$1 trillion earmarked for defense for the first time ever, this budget may see similar contentions. But the DPP seems to be trying to head off criticisms – next year’s budget marks the first time in 78 years that the government budget involves substantive zero net borrowing. 
After many months of contention over Taiwan’s government spending, the pan-Blue camp seemed to finally relent on August 14. The budget was finally passed on that day – 266 days past the deadline, and almost one year after the Executive Yuan originally submitted the budget for consideration on August 29, 2025.
The eventual passage of the budget occurred amid growing concern that defense spending was being held up – especially funding for drones. 
The Kuomintang (KMT) – which currently holds the majority in the legislature along with its third-party ally, the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) – had previously suggested that it would cut funding or impose funding freezes on drone spending, alleging that the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) was using the drone industry to funnel money to untested companies and line its pockets. Reports at the time in pan-Green media outlets also suggested that China hoped to see drone spending blocked and had directed United Front Work Departments to coordinate to influence public opinion in Taiwan. 
However, the KMT seemed to suddenly reverse course after an article in The Economist accused the party of failing to protect Taiwan’s democracy out of the political selfishness of its politicians.
Still, the budget that was passed had substantial cuts, including with regard to drone spending. The cuts amounted to 1.7 percent of the Executive Yuan’s original budget, which KMT legislative caucus leader Fu Kun-chi framed as a generous gesture. By comparison, in 2025, when the KMT instituted the largest set of budget cuts in Taiwanese political history – freezing or cutting one-third of the government’s operational expenses – this was around 3 percent of the proposed budget. 
When it comes to drone funding, the Lai administration originally intended to pass a special budget of NT$210 billion (US$6.6 billion) that would have been used to purchase 1,446 coastal reconnaissance drones, 208,200 coastal attack drones, and 1,320 unmanned surface vessels. The budget would have run from August 2026 through the end of 2031, with spending of NT$42.1 billion per year. Importantly, that would have come on top of NT$31 billion budgeted by the military for unmanned systems as part of its existing budget. 
The budget passed by the KMT allocated NT$240 billion in funding for all purchases of unmanned systems, which will be under the budget for the central government rather than as a separate special budget. Spending would be limited to a cap of NT$40 billion per year, which would be subject to regulatory approval. In other words, the KMT has reduced the budget for military spending on drones from around NT$73 billion a year to NT$40 billion – a 45 percent reduction.
The KMT intends to exert control over the process for drone development through annual approval. Industry experts have warned that this could be detrimental for the long-term development of Taiwan’s drone industry. Building up domestic drone capacity usually requires an initial injection of capital that then tapers off, rather than the same amount of funding year after year. Likewise, drone companies will have to face uncertainty, as the KMT could deny approval for funding in subsequent cycles. 
Some reports suggest that the Executive Yuan will accept the reduced drone budget nonetheless, although it is possible that it may still attempt to fight for additional funding. 
The KMT has sought to deny funding to defense initiatives undertaken by the Tsai and Lai administrations, claiming that effectiveness has not yet been proven. Beyond drones, under the current budget, the KMT has moved to freeze NT$11.9 billion in funding for Taiwan’s domestic submarine program – for the completion of a planned fleet of seven submarines – until after testing for the first submarine of the fleet, the Hai Kun. 
Besides defense programs, the new budget brings other cuts. All media and publicity budgets were slashed by half, while all special operational expenses were but by 60 percent. It is expected that cuts to media and publicity budgets will impact the ability of the government to advertise social services, conduct outreach about civil resilience, and even recruit soldiers.
articles.summary: The budget was passed almost 9 months late, amid growing concern that defense spending was being held up – especially funding for drones.

articles.title: Ethanol Issue Has Entered Indian Kitchens, Impacting Household Budgets
articles.full_text:
What began as an energy policy to reduce crude imports has travelled through the agricultural supply chain and ended up on the dinner table.
India’s ambitious plan to mix ethanol with petrol was touted as the country’s answer to reducing crude-oil imports, saving precious foreign exchange and, above all, bringing down petrol prices. Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari, one of the biggest advocates of ethanol blending, had even said that the use of ethanol would bring down the price of petrol from around 110 Indian rupees or $1.15 per liter at present to just 15 rupees.
Gadkari is not the petroleum minister. His vociferous support for ethanol blending has raised many eyebrows. Opposition parties, including the Congress, have accused him of conflict of interest, alleging that the E20 fuel he is promoting benefits companies owned by his sons. Gadkari has dismissed these allegations as “politically motivated.”
However, instead of conferring benefits on consumers, the introduction of E20, a blend of 20 percent ethanol with petrol, is taking a heavy toll on vehicles and the household budget of middle-class Indians. E20 has had no impact on petrol prices or crude oil imports. On the contrary, it has triggered concerns over mileage, compatibility and its effect on older vehicles. This has forced consumers to opt for ethanol-free, ultra-premium fuel, which is, of course, expensive.
Apart from the economic effect, is its impact on the Narendra Modi government. It is the worst PR disaster the government has ever faced. Social media is flooded with reports of the high cost of ethanol production, besides the huge amount of water usage. According to reports, the average cost of producing or procuring ethanol is around 66 to 72 rupees per liter, which is higher than the refinery cost of around 52 to 55 rupees per liter of pure petrol when crude oil prices are near $70 a barrel.
The public outcry became louder when sugar prices surged dramatically in recent weeks, reaching around 70 rupees a kilogram in some markets. The government has responded by permitting duty-free imports of one million tons of raw sugar — the first such move in nearly a decade. Although the government tried to assure the public that the diversion of sugarcane has declined from around 12 percent in 2022-23 to about 9 percent in 2025-26, the damage was done.
The hue and cry over rising sugar prices had hardly subsided when egg prices rose by around 35-40 percent due to corn being used for ethanol production. Corn is not merely a crop that can be converted into fuel. It is also a crucial ingredient in poultry feed. Recent reports suggest that around 37 percent of India’s corn production is now going to ethanol distilleries. According to the poultry industry, corn accounts for roughly 65-70 percent of poultry production costs. For the first time, India, which was Asia’s top corn exporter, has become a net importer.
Recent reports suggest that around 37 percent of India’s corn production is now going to ethanol distilleries. Nitin Gupta of Olam Agri India says the poultry and starch industries are “battling with distilleries to get their share of supplies, and this fight is keeping prices high.”
And once corn becomes more expensive, the impact does not stop with corn alone. It enters the food chain. Egg prices have risen by around 35-40 percent over the past year, according to industry data. The same corn-based feed is used by broiler chickens raised for meat. So, when the cost of poultry feed rises, the cost of producing chicken rises too.
What began as an energy policy has therefore travelled through the agricultural supply chain and ended up on the dinner table. That is the real danger. One diversion can affect the entire food chain. And corn may not be the end of the story.
India has also allowed rice to be used as an ethanol feedstock, including rice from the Food Corporation of India’s stocks. The government has defended the policy by arguing that it uses surplus grain and gives farmers an additional market.
The danger is not necessarily that every grain will suddenly disappear into an ethanol plant. The danger is that diverting one commodity can set off a chain reaction across several others.
That is a dangerous connection. The world has seen this before. India is not the first country to discover that the road from the petrol pump to the dinner table can be surprisingly short.
During the global food-price crisis of 2007-08, the rapid expansion of biofuels was identified by economists as one of several factors behind the dramatic rise in food prices.
There were many causes: high oil prices, droughts, declining grain stocks, rising demand and export restrictions. But the conversion of food crops into fuel created another powerful source of demand.
Agricultural economists C. Ford Runge and Benjamin Senauer warned in 2007 that the diversion of corn into ethanol was sending “shock waves through the food system.”

Mexico’s dependence on corn as a staple food meant that the increase quickly translated into higher tortilla prices. In early 2007, the country witnessed demonstrations over the rising cost of tortillas.
In April 2008, in Haiti, protesters angry over soaring food prices attempted to storm the presidential palace in Port-au-Prince. U.N. peacekeepers fired tear gas and rubber bullets to push them back. Haiti’s prime minister was subsequently forced from office.

articles.title: Despite Delays, China Could Gain Ground in the Space Race
articles.full_text:
While the U.S. still holds considerable advantages gained through its earlier lunar explorations, China’s planned mission could provide it with a crucial edge.
China abruptly postponed its planned Chang’e 7 lunar launch, which was scheduled to take place on August 24. While the new launch timeline is unclear, the mission could still be a significant step in the U.S.-China space race.
The launch was initially scheduled for August 23 before being rescheduled for a day later and eventually postponed indefinitely. Some outlets have reported poor weather as a reason for the delay, but official statements have given limited details, saying that the lunar expedition “failed to meet launch criteria.”
It’s now less clear whether China will return to the lunar surface before the United States. If it can, it may be able to gain advantages in areas such as resource mapping and the reshaping of norms, supporting Beijing to pursue its ambitions in outer space. While the U.S. still holds considerable advantages gained through its earlier lunar explorations, this mission could provide China with a crucial edge.
The uncrewed mission aims to search the lunar surface for water ice. It includes an orbiter, lander, a small hopping probe and a rover, all launched on a Long March 5 rocket to a landing site near the southeast ridge of the Shackleton crater on the lunar south pole. Another key objective is to explore the area’s suitability as the site of a planned lunar research base.
In 2021, China and Russia announced a new lunar initiative: a crewed lunar base called the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS), which is meant to be a crewed lunar base. This was to be led by the China National Space Administration and Russia’s Roscosmos. China and Russia plan for this base to facilitate further exploration of the Moon, including possible resource utilisation.
The Chang’e 7 mission also includes six international partners conducting their own experiments, including Russia and Egypt. Several U.S. allies and partners are also taking part, such as Bahrain, Italy, Thailand, and Switzerland as well as a Hawaii-based non-government organization. The inclusion of such a diverse set of partners is indicative of China’s efforts to conduct space diplomacy and generate soft power benefits. It may also be intended to give additional legitimacy to Chinese lunar projects, especially if those projects were to veer into areas that could raise questions, such as lunar mining.
But the mission’s primary aim will be finding water ice. If China can confirm the presence of water ice, it could potentially convert the substance into drinking water and oxygen to support human inhabitation. The ice could also be split into hydrogen and oxygen rocket fuel, which could open the possibility of converting the ILRS into a base for inter-planetary missions. Both advances would give China a significant leg-up in its space race with the United States.
This ongoing space race gives the Chang’e 7 launch great strategic importance. China’s advantage has been increased by ongoing interruptions to U.S. lunar missions – NASA’s Viper program, which has similar objectives to the Chang’e mission and was meant to launch in 2024, is now planned for 2027 at the earliest. The data that these missions aim to gather could possibly fuel future missions. This is one reason why such lunar missions are valuable and why both the U.S. and China are aiming for the same real estate. China is also preparing for a follow-on mission, the Chang’e 8, which is slated for 2028. However, it’s unclear how today’s delay will affect this timeline. These two missions will allow China to make significant progress towards establishing its lunar base.
Whoever gets to the Moon first in this leg of the space race will benefit from first-mover advantages. This will include gaining the upper hand in resource mapping and studying the lunar environment. If China gets there first, we can expect an effort to frame norms and standards for lunar exploration in a manner that is going to be particularly beneficial to Beijing. While the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 prohibits states from making sovereignty claims, the treaty doesn’t cover resource mining. China could try to frame new rules and norms while seeking support from other countries. One can only imagine the huge soft power advantage Beijing could garner. The symbolism and soft power aspects of China’s lunar activities shouldn’t be dismissed, as they have strategic undercurrents.
Whether others will catch up remains to be seen. This includes the United States. NASA’s Artemis IV and V, which are supposed to be crewed lunar landing missions, are currently planned for early and late 2028. China appears to have a head start, but in terms of crewed landing and exploration on the Moon, the U.S. could still have an advantage, particularly after the Chang’e-7 postponement. The real problem is that the U.S. appears somewhat distracted and less determined than China has been on this issue. Whether this can be overcome is anybody’s guess.
This article was originally published in ASPI’s The Strategist.

articles.title: India, China Take Small Step Forward Toward Border Settlement
articles.full_text:
At the recent special representatives talks in Beijing, the two sides agreed to work on identifying less contentious sections of their disputed border.
Indian and Chinese delegations at the 25th Meeting of Special Representatives on the India-China Boundary Question held in Beijing, China, on Aug. 25, 2026.
Top officials of India and China have agreed to work on identifying less contentious sections of their contested border for delimitation as part of a broader process toward resolving their longstanding boundary dispute.
A special group of negotiators will identify these less disputed parts of the border and delimit them, a joint statement released on August 26 said. The statement came a day after India’s National Security Adviser Ajit Doval met China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing for talks. Doval and Wang are the designated special representatives of their two countries for the boundary talks mechanism, which was established in 2003 to address the border dispute.
At the talks in Beijing, India and China also agreed to two new military hotlines in the eastern and middle sections of their border and two new meeting points for military commander-level interactions to immediately deal with any tensions that arise along their 3,500 km-long border. Officials of the two countries will meet next month to discuss issues related to trans-border rivers as they look to take their relationship forward after ties sank to a six-decade low during the June 2020 Galwan clash.
“The two sides agreed that any situation on the ground would be addressed promptly through existing diplomatic and military channels,” the statement, which listed eight outcomes, said. The emphasis was on stabilizing the border and ensuring that any tensions that surface are defused before they impact the larger relationship.
“The two sides discussed ways to improve understanding of LAC [Line of Actual Control, the de facto border] in appropriate areas, for better border management,” it said. This is a key outcome given that differing perceptions of where the border lies have been the principal source of friction between the countries.
There was agreement on maintaining peace and tranquility along the border and on creating “an atmosphere for healthy and steady development of bilateral relations,” the joint statement said. India has stated multiple times that peace on the border was a pre-requisite for progress in other areas of the China-India bilateral relationship, such as economic engagement.
The two countries said they were committed to finding a solution to their vexed boundary problem based on a 2005 pact that says the final agreement would be a “package settlement” that would cover the entire border – the western, middle, and eastern sections. The 2005 pact also provides for both countries to “safeguard due interests of their settled populations in the border areas.”
India has been particularly keen that the solution to border tensions with China be a comprehensive one, covering the entire stretch of the border rather than selected areas seen as easier to resolve. Moreover, some of these areas with easier resolution prospects are also ones where India holds a military advantage vis-a-vis China.
The joint statement was issued a day after the two countries put out separate readouts of their talks, which was taken as a sign that the two countries were far apart on key issues. The release of the joint statement has set at rest doubts that differences had outweighed points of agreement.
The China-India talks come against the backdrop of an increasingly unstable world order where the United States is seen as an inward-looking and unreliable partner. Previously, India had perceived the U.S. as a hedge against China’s growing assertiveness in Asia. India views China as its principal long-term adversary. However, New Delhi has been at the receiving end of Donald Trump’s tariffs and other punitive measures over the past year. Consequently, India is adopting an “America Plus” strategy that includes outreach to countries and groups like Japan, the European Union, Russia and China, said security affairs analyst C. Raja Mohan, in an article in the Foreign Affairs magazine.
C. Uday Bhaskar, a retired commodore of the Indian Navy and currently director at the Society for Policy Studies think tank in New Delhi, noted that a joint statement after talks between special representatives of India and China on border issues was “rare.” “This time, an eight-point text was actually agreed within 18 hours, which signals political intent at the highest level to lock in stability ahead of a packed fortnight,” he said in a recent opinion piece. The delay in issuing the eight-point document was symptomatic of what defines China-India relations currently — “deeply embedded wariness,” he added.
The Doval-Wang talks set the stage for the upcoming meetings between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at two summits over the coming fortnight: the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Summit at Bishkek on August 31-September 1 and the India-chaired meeting of the BRICS countries in New Delhi on September 12-13.
Xi is expected to travel to India for the BRICS meet, although Beijing has not announced the visit yet. It will be his first visit to India since 2019.
The move toward a rapprochement amid simmering tensions along the LAC triggered by the Galwan clashes began in 2024 with India and China announcing the pull back of troops from close proximity along border points in Eastern Ladakh, high up in the Himalayas. Indian and Chinese troops are now disengaged, i.e. no longer in close proximity to each other, but they are yet to move back to peacetime positions. This means that neither side has de-escalated deployment as yet.
Modi and Xi have met on two occasions since the disengagement of troops – in Kazan in Russia on the sidelines of the 2024 BRICS summit and on the margins of the China-hosted SCO summit in Tianjin last year.
Meanwhile, the two sides have acted to resume connectivity; travel woes have eased and airlines have resumed flights.
News reports suggest that India and China are exploring new ways to facilitate business-to-business exchanges with India aiming to attract Chinese investments. Some of these announcements could be made when Xi lands in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.
Earlier this year, India amended the rules allowing easier investment flows from China after tightening rules in 2020. India sees increased investments from China as a way to cut down its ballooning trade deficit with Beijing.
With a goal to become a developed economy by 2047, India is looking for investments, technology, and ways to boost its manufacturing. With Trump making the U.S. an unreliable partner and India looking at other partners to fill the void, China next door has emerged a real possibility.
“We are not in the 1991 world,” where there was only one superpower — the United States, Atul Aneja, a former correspondent of The Hindu in Beijing, told The Diplomat. “Today’s world is a multipolar world. There is China, Russia, and others. Power is fragmented and that is reflected in the change of character of global power system. In this scenario, India needs to engage with China,” he said.
India’s outreach to China comes against the backdrop of Beijing’s mounting military and economic support to India’s archrival, Pakistan, on many occasions. There is also concern in New Delhi over China’s propensity to weaponize supply chains, i.e., to stop export of key products that India’s economy is dependent on. Beijing’s sudden halt of fertilizer exports to India is a case in point.
While China is seeking increased access to India’s market for its electric vehicle (EV) manufacturers, news reports suggest that China is reluctant to transfer EV battery technology to Indian businesses. Indian companies are also reportedly struggling to obtain rare earth magnets from China, with restrictions first noticed in April 2025.
All this suggests India’s rapprochement with China isn’t likely to be smooth or straightforward. While it is in India’s national interests to seek out Chinese investments, Beijing would definitely seek a bigger footprint for its businesses in India. But it seems doubtful that Beijing would greenlight technology transfers or move to build up India, given that Delhi is a potential challenger to China’s Asian and global ambitions in the future.

articles.title: Vietnam’s Expanding Strategic Partnerships: Why Canada Could Be Next
articles.full_text:
Recent developments suggest that the two middle-powers are on the cusp of an important diplomatic upgrade.
Canadian Ambassador Jim Nickel presents his diplomatic credentials to Vietnamese President Luong Cuong in Hanoi, Vietnam, Oct. 3, 2025.
Vietnam organizes its foreign relations into a three-tier hierarchy: Comprehensive Partnerships (CPs) sit at the base, Strategic Partnerships (SPs) in the middle, and Comprehensive Strategic Partnerships (CSPs) at the top. This sits alongside a category of special relationships with Cold War-era allies Laos, Cambodia, and Cuba.
Hanoi’s “bamboo diplomacy,” flexible in form but firm at its roots, has expanded all three categories at a remarkable pace. As of early 2026, Vietnam has 15 CSPs, following the upgrade of relations with the European Union in January 2026, alongside 15 SPs and 17 CPs. This network now touches every continent and every major power center, from Washington and Beijing to Moscow, Brussels, London, and Canberra.
The question that naturally follows is: who is next? Vietnam has not filled every available slot on its diplomatic hierarchy, and Hanoi has made clear – through the CPTPP chairmanship it holds in 2026 and the APEC hosting role it takes on in 2027 – that it intends to keep climbing. There are three reasons why Canada may be the next nation in line for a diplomatic upgrade.
The first is structural. Vietnam’s diplomatic strategy increasingly resembles that of other “middle powers” – states too large to be ignored but not seeking hegemony, which instead build resilience through diversified, non-aligned partnerships. Analysts have already grouped Vietnam alongside Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, and Switzerland as countries capable of maintaining deep ties with rival great powers simultaneously. If Vietnam is consciously cultivating this identity, it has an incentive to deepen ties specifically with other middle powers that share its instinct for strategic autonomy rather than bloc alignment — and Canada is one of the clearest examples of that category on the world stage today.
The second reason is geographic. Vietnam’s CSP network is heavily concentrated in Asia and Europe. Of its 30 SPs and CSPs, only two are in the Americas: the United States as a CSP and Brazil as an SP. For a country pursuing “multi-directional” diplomacy and actively courting new markets to reduce its dependence on any single economy, this is a conspicuous gap. Creating a second North American SP or CSP would meaningfully reduce the imbalance and enhance Vietnam’s global footprint and give it a more credible claim to truly global reach.
Third, Vietnam already holds strategic-level partnerships with six of the seven G-7 members, namely the United States (CSP), Japan (CSP), Germany (SP), France (CSP), the United Kingdom (CSP), and Italy (SP). Canada is the only G7 economy with which Vietnam has not yet formalized a strategic-tier relationship; the two countries currently sit at the lower “Comprehensive Partnership” level. In the meantime, Vietnam’s foreign policy attaches importance to promoting relationships with “major powers and important partners.” Obviously, Vietnam sees Canada as “an important partner.”
Taken together, these three reasons converge on a single conclusion: among Vietnam’s plausible next upgrades, Canada is the most logical choice.
Indeed, what makes this more than a hypothesis is that Hanoi and Ottawa are visibly moving in this direction already. In January 2026, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered a widely noted address describing a “rupture” in the rules-based international order and calling on middle powers to cooperate more closely to protect their interests as great-power rivalry intensifies. His argument – that middle powers need to band together as the old order frays — dovetails almost precisely with the logic Vietnam has been applying to its own diplomacy.
On the Vietnamese side, the signals have been just as direct. On June 29, Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung told Canada’s ambassador that Hanoi “always regards Canada as an important partner” and pressed for expanded cooperation in trade, artificial intelligence, quantum technology and semiconductors. Hung also told the guest that Vietnam “wishes to elevate ties with Canada to a new level.”  In the meantime, Vietnam’s National Assembly Chairman voiced confidence that the two sides would bring their partnership “to new heights.”
Most recently, on August 22, Vietnam’s Foreign Minister asked his Canadian counterpart “to work closely to materialize the upgrade of ties as anticipated by leaders of both sides.” The Canadian Foreign Minister responded positively. Both capitals are actively laying groundwork for an upgrade.
The upgrade of ties is not a one-way wish. In fact, the logic runs both ways. Canada is a developed, technologically advanced economy that can support Vietnam’s ambitious “centennial” development goals – Hanoi’s targets, tied to the 2030 and 2045 anniversaries of the Communist Party and the state, for becoming a high-income, technology-driven nation. Canadian officials have flagged priority cooperation areas including AI, semiconductors, nuclear energy, aerospace, and high-quality workforce training – precisely the sectors Vietnam needs to climb the value chain.
Trade figures reinforce the case. Vietnam is now Canada’s largest trading partner within ASEAN, and bilateral merchandise trade has grown rapidly. Two-way trade reached roughly $15.7 billion in 2024 by Canadian measures, with Vietnam’s exports to Canada surpassing $10 billion for the first time that year. Growth has continued into 2026, driven increasingly by machinery, electronics and other high-value goods rather than low-cost manufactures – a shift that signals a maturing, higher-value trade relationship. The first seven months of 2026 saw Vietnam’s cumulative export value to Canada exceed $5 billion, an increase of more than 20 percent over the same period in 2025. For Vietnam, Canada represents both a resilient market amid global trade uncertainty and a hedge against overreliance on the United States, especially as Washington’s tariff policies have grown less predictable.
None of the above-mentioned arguments and figures guarantee a diplomatic upgrade is imminent. Vietnam moves deliberately, and any new CSP or SP requires sustained high-level engagement. But the underlying structural logic, the rhetorical alignment between the two sides, and the diplomatic signaling from both Hanoi and Ottawa in 2026 suggest that such a move may just be a matter of time.

articles.title: Indonesia, United States Kick Off Annual Multinational Military Exercises
articles.full_text:
Super Garuda Shield 2026 will involve more than 4,700 troops from 13 nations, and observers from a further eight others.
U.S., Indonesian, and South Korean marines, as well as personnel from the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force, stand at attention during an opening ceremony for Exercise Super Garuda Shield 26 at the Indonesian Marine Corps 7th Infantry Battalion base near Lampung, Indonesia, Aug. 31, 2026.
The United States and Indonesia launched annual multilateral military exercises yesterday, which the two sides said aimed to improve interoperability and bolster deterrence in the region.
Super Garuda Shield, which has been held annually since 2007, will take place in various locations including Bandung, Lampung, Kalimantan, and the Indonesian Army’s Baturaja Combat Training Center in South Sumatra before concluding in Jakarta on September 11.
This year’s iteration will involve more than 4,743 personnel from 13 other countries including Japan, ​South Korea, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. A further eight nations will join as observers. While the total number of troops is slightly down on last year’s iteration, which featured a record 5,400 participants, it includes more participating nations than ever, with India taking part as an observer for the first time.
Major General Patrick Ellis, the commanding general of the U.S. Army’s 4th Infantry Division, said that the exercise was critical for “building the human architecture that keeps the Indo-Pacific safe.”
“The security landscape of the Indo-Pacific is complex and readiness cannot be surged when a crisis begins,” he said at an opening ceremony at the Indonesian Armed Forces’ School of Command in Bandung. He added, “We are not just meeting for another annual training cycle. We are writing a historic new chapter in our ​bilateral relationship.”
TNI Commander General Agus Subiyanto, the commander of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, said that “the purpose of the exercise is, first, diplomacy, and then cooperation through the exchange of capabilities.”
The Garuda Shield exercise was established between the U.S. and Indonesian militaries in 2007 and forms a primary pillar of the two nations’ defense relationship. “Super” was added to its title in 2022, when the exercise was expanded into a multilateral format.
This year, the exercises “will include a joint staff exercise, cyber exercise, airborne operations, jungle training, and amphibious exercise,” the U.S. Army said in a statement.  U.S. Navy and U.S. Coast Guard personnel will also conduct coordinated maritime training serials with the Indonesian Navy in adjacent waters in order “to strengthen joint interoperability at sea.”
Participating forces will also take part in special forces infiltration drills, cyber defense exercises, the firing of Stinger missiles, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief operations.
The expanded exercise is the first to take place since Indonesia and the U.S. established a new defense cooperation pact in April. The Major Defense Cooperation Partnership (MDCP) will bolster cooperation in Indonesian military modernization and increase training, joint exercises, and professional military education, with the aim of “maintaining peace and stability” in Asia.
Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth said at the time that they “have also committed to enhance joint special forces training,” and to expand existing multilateral exercises, including Super Garuda Shield.
The continued expansion of the annual exercise speaks to the continued good health of the U.S.-Indonesia defense partnership, which has remained stable despite the erratic nature of foreign policymaking under the second Trump administration. However, while Indonesia has welcomed closer U.S. security cooperation, it continues to hew to a policy of foreign policy non-alignment, and to maintain a balanced spread of defense engagements – including with key U.S. adversaries.
For example, on the same day that Sjafrie and Hegseth signed the MDCP agreement in Jakarta, President Prabowo Subianto was being hosted at the Kremlin by Russian President Vladimir Putin.
And last month, Indonesia agreed to boost its military ties with China during a visit to Jakarta by the country’s foreign and ​defense ministers. The two sides agreed to increase joint exercises and officer exchanges. They also discussed the establishment of a joint munitions factory in Indonesia that would include a possible transfer of technology from China. Also in August, Jakarta courted controversy when an Indonesian frigate conducted a joint navigation exercise with China’s People’s Liberation Army Navy in the waters east of Taiwan – the first time that China had exercised with a foreign military in the area.
Later this year, China and Indonesia are scheduled to hold their Heping Garuda joint military exercises, which took place for the first time in December 2024. These much narrower drills will focus mostly on humanitarian aid and disaster relief operations.

articles.title: Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing to Visit Vietnam Soon, State Media Says
articles.full_text:
All four mainland Southeast Asian states have now extended an official invitation to the general-turned-president since his inauguration in April.
Myanmar’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, will soon visit Vietnam, his fourth visit to an ASEAN member state since taking office in April, Myanmar state media reported today.
According to a report in the Global New Light of Myanmar, the former general will travel to Vietnam “in the near future” at the invitation of To Lam, Vietnam’s president and the head of the Communist Party of Vietnam. In addition to meeting with Lam, he will also meet with Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh and Tran Thanh Man, the head of the National Assembly, and “receive representatives from economic organizations.”
“During the visit, the President will hold cordial discussions and exchange views on further consolidation of the existing friendly relations…  as well as cooperation across economic, cultural, and various other sectors,” the report stated.
The announcement, which has not yet been confirmed by Hanoi, comes shortly after Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung traveled to Myanmar last week, the first time that a Vietnamese foreign minister has visited the country since the 2021 coup. During talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyidaw, he “discussed boosting bilateral trade and investment, as well as mutual support on the international stage,” The Irrawaddy reported, citing state media.
Trung also met Lower House speaker Khin Yi and Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, to whom he pledged “continued support for Myanmar at the U.N., ASEAN, and other international forums.” Trung also reportedly extended a formal invitation for Min Aung Hlaing to visit Hanoi.
The trip would be the former general’s fourth to an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member state since taking office as president in April, after visits to Laos in early July and Thailand last month and an upcoming trip to Cambodia in early September. He has also made state visits to India and China in June, and to Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan last month.
All of this reflects a concerted push by Min Aung Hlaing to consolidate Myanmar’s relationship with key partners. A top priority, which he mentioned in his inauguration speech in April, is to normalize relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Since late 2021, the 11-nation bloc has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government, which was formed after flawed multi-phase elections in December and January, has taken an increasingly defiant line toward ASEAN, dismissing the Five-Point Consensus as an unwarranted “interference” in its internal affairs and demanding its full readmission to the bloc.
At the same time, it has sought to engage directly with willing ASEAN member states, particularly Thailand, which has positioned itself as a bridge between Myanmar and ASEAN. During Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Bangkok last month, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul “reaffirmed” Thailand’s commitment “to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.”
The fact that all four of Myanmar’s mainland Southeast Asian neighbors have now extended invitations to Min Aung Hlaing to visit reflects a growing regional fatigue with the Myanmar conflict, and a belief that “calibrated reengagement” (in Thailand’s phrase) is the best way to manage the effects of the civil war, if not to resolve it.
It also reflects a continuing divergence between ASEAN’s mainland and maritime member states on how to deal with Myanmar. Over the past five years, the mainland states have favored more engagement than maritime nations such as Singapore, Indonesia, and Malaysia, which have advocated a more robust regional response to the military coup in Myanmar. Whether and to what extent Myanmar manages to make inroads into this camp, which is reportedly also growing with the protracted deadlock inside Myanmar, may become clear in the run-up to the next ASEAN summit in November.

articles.title: The ‘Unique’ Communications That Saved Lives Before Nepal’s Devastating Flood
articles.full_text:
Survivors and experts say that instant word-of-mouth warnings may have saved hundreds of lives on August 26.
A view of Langtang Lirung, a mountain in Langtang National Park, Nepal, from the southeast. A glacier collapse on the north face of the mountain is believed to be the proximate cause of the devastating flash floods on August 26, 2026.
Families and experts in Nepal have told of the devastating flood that killed over 900 and the little-known cultural phenomenon that may have saved even more lives from being lost.
According to those on the ground, while the waters surged through villages and left over 4,200 missing around the border between Nepal and China, some families had advanced warning of the imminent disaster.
“In Nepal, people-to-people information sharing is quite good and also a unique phenomenon,” Dr Basanta Raj Adhikari, the director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at the Institute of Engineering at Tribhuvan University in Kirtipur, Kathmandu, told The Diplomat.
According to Adhikari, in times of an environmental disaster such as an earthquake, landslide, or flood such as the one witnessed on August 26, news travels fast, with villages higher up in the mountains quickly passing information to those in the lower lands, and warning residents that danger is on the way.
“People upstream give information to those lower down so that they can save themselves,” Basanta said.
This informal method of sounding the alarm appears to have worked for some families along the Trishuli River where the flood waters arose. These included Rita Tamang, who lives in Daring, Gajuri, along the Prithvi Highway which sits beside the waterway.
“Before the flood came, we had moved a little higher up from our house, but we still witnessed the flood very clearly. It was absolutely terrifying. The flood was not just carrying a huge amount of water; it was also sweeping away all kinds of things, causing massive destruction. Our house was also badly damaged, with almost half of it destroyed,” the 34-year-old housewife told The Diplomat.
“We knew about the flood coming from Rasuwagadhi about two to four hours beforehand. But we had never seen a flood this severe and terrifying before. In fact, we had never witnessed anything like this in our lives.”
Tamang said that the flood completely washed away three concrete bridges that vehicles used to cross the river, and destroyed a key suspension bridge in the area.
It was Tamang’s brother, 32-year-old Bikram Tamang, who helped to save her life.
Bikram Tamang said that he had been at the China-Nepal border working as a truck driver and transporting goods from the border to Kathmandu, Birgunj, Pokhara, and other cities in Nepal.
After delivering the goods, drivers usually return with empty trucks, Tamang said, and Bikram had just dropped off a delivery when he got news of a torrent of water approaching.
“His friends informed him that a dam had apparently burst and that a massive flood had come. They told everyone to stay safe and not to go near the riverbank,” she said. “From there, my brother directly called us at home, and that is how we came to know about the flood.”
It is thought that the Nepal flood wave was caused by a glacial collapse after a large chunk of ice from a glacier broke off and fell into a river. This ice then melted, mixing with river water and debris, before gushing through mountain gulleys and destroying villages, towns, bridges, roads, and homes.
As a result of the advanced warning from her younger sibling, Tamang and her family were able to scramble to higher ground.
Both Basanta and Tamang said that, in times of disaster, word-of-mouth was often faster than official warnings, although Tamang explained that both Ncell and Namaste, two major telecommunications networks in Nepal, had managed to send alerts to their subscribers that a major flood had occurred.
The alerts also advised residents to evacuate areas along the Trishuli River.
However, both Basanta and Tamang said that time was of the essence when a disaster occurred as both internet and phone signals were disrupted once power lines were destroyed.
Basanta added that the risk of secondary flooding from lakes swelling upstream and bursting was an ongoing threat, and that it would be a consideration for search and rescue teams looking for survivors and the deceased. However, the information and people-to-people sharing that was used when the first flood happened would likely be harnessed again by those working in the area.
“The Nepal government is aware of the risks and is working closely to get information from those upstream to those lower down,” Dr Basanta said.
He explained that there would be a similar chain of information sharing by the local authorities, using other devices such as satellite phones or walkie-talkies, that would allow those working on higher ground to warn if more floods were coming, in the event that normal phone lines and internet were still disrupted.
Following the first wave, the fear that more floods would follow came to fruition for Tamang, who said that many families were choosing to sleep outside their homes in case rising waters caused buildings to wash away completely.
“On Sunday, the flood came again at around five in the morning and, on Saturday, a very large flood came from the stream near our village which forced many families to leave their homes,” she said.
She added that they were safe for now but that, with every new wave of water, the family had to move to higher ground and wait for it to subside before returning to their partially damaged home.
“People are in a very difficult situation. Most of their belongings are outside and they have nowhere safe to stay. There are children, elderly people, parents, and people with disabilities among them.”
And while Tamang’s brother Bikram was initially able to make contact and urge his family to seek shelter, communication has now completely ceased, even though internet and phone connections have been restored in her area.
“As far as we know, he was in contact with his family until he had loaded his vehicle inside the Chinese border area and was about to leave. There has been no information about his whereabouts or condition,” Tamang said.
“We don’t know whether he is alive, safe, or what has happened to him. We have tried repeatedly to contact him, but his mobile phone is completely unreachable.”
articles.summary: Survivors and experts say that instant word-of-mouth warnings may have saved hundreds of lives on August 26.

articles.title: How Great Power Rivalry Is Fracturing the Pacific Islands Forum
articles.full_text:
Absences from this year’s Leaders’ Meeting are raising questions about the group’s solidarity amid growing China-U.S. competition.
The Smaller Island States (SIS) Leaders Meeting kicks off the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting week in Palau, Aug. 31, 2026.
The 55th Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders’ Meeting opened on August 31 under a banner of unity, but it can’t escape the reality that outside powers are competing for influence in the Pacific. The question now facing the PIF is whether the forum’s consensus model, once a safeguard for small-state sovereignty, has become the very mechanism through which that influence reshapes regional outcomes.
The official theme of this year’s PIF Leaders’ Meeting, held in Palau, is B.E.L.A.U., or Building Economies, Life, Action, Unity, an acronym that doubles as a tribute to the host nation’s indigenous name. It was meant to signal collective resolve. Instead, the gathering has been defined by conspicuous absences and blocked consensus. Given the return of Taiwan as a development partner after last year’s exclusion, some see this year’s PIF as proof of Beijing’s growing capacity to paralyze the region’s most important multilateral institution from within.
At least five Pacific leaders chose not to attend. The leaders of Kiribati, Samoa, and Vanuatu dispatched deputies, while Fiji’s Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka stayed home to manage domestic affairs. The most dramatic absence was that of Solomon Islands’ Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who landed in Palau only to leave hours later after a no-confidence motion was filed against him back in Honiara. Wale had served as prime minister for barely three months and as outgoing PIF chair, was meant to hand the gavel to Palau’s President Surangel Whipps Jr. Instead, he left Foreign Minister Rick Hou to represent his country at the summit.
Kiribati’s case is particularly revealing. President Taneti Maamau dispatched not a cabinet minister but David Teaabo, his director of foreign service and a former ambassador to China. In an organization where decisions require consensus at the level of heads of state, sending a lower-ranking delegate who cannot commit to communique language with full authority is itself a political statement.
Kiribati’s posture becomes clearer against the backdrop of the missile crisis that preceded the summit. On July 6, China conducted a submarine-launched ballistic missile test in the Pacific, firing what Taiwan identified as a JL-2 from the South China Sea. The missile, carrying a dummy warhead, transited the exclusive economic zones of the Federated States of Micronesia, Naoero (formerly Nauru), and Kiribati before landing near Tuvalu’s maritime boundary. Beijing provided only a few hours’ notice to the affected Pacific Island nations.
The reaction was swift – at least from those countries that did respond. Papua New Guinea’s Prime Minister James Marape invoked the region’s traumatic history of nuclear testing, insisting that Pacific nations “do not want history repeated.” Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the test “provocative” and “destabilizing.” Yet when Pacific foreign ministers gathered in Fiji in early August, Kiribati and Naoero blocked the consensus needed to issue a joint condemnation.
The PIF has historically operated on the principle of unanimity, a practice rooted in what Pacific leaders call the “Pacific Way,” designed to ensure that no island nation, however small, could be overruled by its larger neighbors. But the model assumed that external pressures would remain at the margins of PIF deliberations. When a member state with deep ties to the power responsible for a security event deploys its consensus rights to shield that power from collective criticism, the model risks becoming a means of undermining collective action.
New Zealand’s Foreign Minister Winston Peters made the frustration explicit, noting that two countries “were seeking to use the need for consensus as a veto provision.” Peters said that he had “made it very clear that we didn’t think outsiders should be telling insiders” what positions to take.
Kiribati’s alignment with Beijing extends beyond the blocking of a PIF statement. In late August, its parliament passed the first reading of a constitutional amendment that would restrict diplomatic recognition to states holding U.N. membership or permanent observer status, effectively locking future governments into recognizing Beijing. Graeme Smith of the Australian National University characterized the move as “almost entirely about sending a message to Beijing.”
With that in mind, Taiwan’s return to the PIF may also have contributed to Kiribati’s lack of top-level representation. 
Last year, when the Solomon Islands hosted the 54th PIF Leaders’ Meeting, all external partners were excluded. The stated reason was a review of partnership arrangements, but the practical effect was to remove Taiwan from a gathering it had attended as a development partner since 1992. This year, with Palau – which has official diplomatic ties with Taiwan – as host, the dynamics reversed. 
Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung arrived in Koror leading a delegation that included representatives from energy, technology, construction, and agriculture, and he met with Whipps, Palau’s president, to strengthen bilateral ties before participating in the Taiwan/Republic of China-Forum Countries Dialogue. 
Only three PIF members still maintain formal ties with Taipei, but Taiwan’s development programs extend well beyond those allies. Just in July 2026, Taiwan donated $2 million to the Forum Secretariat and in 2025 it pledged $3 million to the Pacific Resilience Facility. 
Beijing, however, doesn’t take kindly to Taiwan’s inclusion in any form. China’s special envoy Qian Bo confronted Whipps directly at the Forum Troika meeting in Fiji, demanding Taiwan’s exclusion and warning that Beijing would “have to retaliate.” He dismissed Palau as “a small country.” Whipps was unfazed: “It doesn’t matter. We’re a country.” He later characterized Qian’s conduct as inappropriate, remarking that “if you want somebody to love you, usually you come with chocolates and nice cards.”
China made good on Qian’s threat on August 19, when Beijing’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism issued a travel advisory for Palau, warning of alleged theft and dangerous marine conditions and portraying one of the Pacific’s safest destinations as a place to avoid. The U.S. Embassy rejected the advisory, stating that “the United States opposes any attempts by China to weaponize tourism to coerce Palau.”
Tourism accounts for roughly 40 percent of Palau’s gross domestic product, and Beijing has used this lever before. After Palau refused to break ties with Taiwan, China banned package tours in 2017 and visitor numbers collapsed, but the country absorbed the shock and the weapon’s effectiveness has diminished with repeated use.
Whipps has been characteristically blunt about the situation “China continues to try to influence us, whether its threatening us with weaponizing tourism or attacking us personally,” he told reporters. “We’ve made it very clear from the beginning [that] nobody is going to tell us who our friends can be.”
Palau, with a population of roughly 18,000, has held its ground on Taiwan. Other Pacific Island states haven’t. Solomon Islands switched recognition to Beijing in 2019; Kiribati followed within weeks. Naoero switched in January 2024. Taiwan’s Pacific footprint has halved, going from six diplomatic partners in 2019 to just three today: the Marshall Islands, Palau, and Tuvalu.
The PIF Leaders’ Meeting, of course, is about much more than Taiwan, or even China. The summit’s agenda includes a climate declaration ahead of COP31 and a new maritime anti-smuggling initiative called Waqa Moana. The Pacific Resilience Facility, with $173 million in pledges toward a $500 million target, represents a genuine institutional innovation as a Pacific-owned climate finance mechanism. 
But the credibility of a regional body rests on its capacity to address threats as well as opportunities. A forum that can mobilize around climate finance but cannot issue a statement when a nuclear-armed power tests a ballistic missile in its own members’ waters with barely any warning faces a fundamental question about what regional solidarity actually means. 
The empty chairs in Palau are symptoms of a regional order under pressure, one in which the line between domestic sovereignty and external manipulation grows harder to draw with each passing year.
